title: Timing Plan
text: The workshop runs for 180 minutes, including one 10-minute break. The table counts elapsed time from the start. Adjust the clock times to suit your session.

title: Timing Plan
section: Where to Cut When You Run Late
text:
Where to Cut When You Run Late
Cut in this order. Each cut saves time without removing the verification step, which the workshop depends on.

Episode 09, write task. Set it as homework. Learners still review the flawed script in class.
Episode 07, t-test section. Keep the lm() model and the summary() walk-through. Move the t-test to homework.
Episode 02, scenario cards. Use three of the eight cards, not all eight. Choose Card 1 (the overnight session), Card 2 (the patient records) and Card 4 (the SSH key).
Episode 01, disclosure draft. Ask learners to write it after the session. Show one example in class.
Episode 05, extra debugging. Skip the optional debugging step. Keep the base R cross-check.
Episode 08, chunk options. Give learners the chunk options as a handout.

Do not cut the Check it steps in episodes 04, 05, 06 and 08. Learners who skip them produce reports that are not reliable.
Break rule. If you are more than 10 minutes behind at the break, shorten the break to 5 minutes. Do not drop a whole episode to make up the time.
Catch-up rule. A learner who falls behind copies the checkpoint for the episode they missed from r/checkpoints/ (Python: python/checkpoints/) and carries on. Do not wait for them.
Episode 10 is fixed. Keep it to 5 minutes, even if the session runs late. Its checklist is short, so learners can finish it later.

Language and tone

NZ English spelling (organise, colour, behaviour). Use te reo Māori where natural (Aotearoa New Zealand), with correct macrons.
Plain, direct and active voice. Address the learner as “you”. No marketing language.
Assume a researcher who knows base R, data frames and basic ggplot2 (GA Introduction to R), but has not used pipes, dplyr or Quarto.
Tool-agnostic: say “your AI assistant”. Track A demos use Google Search AI Mode. Never claim a specific AI response. AI output varies, so describe typical failure patterns (“often…”, “may…”).

title: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code
text:
This page is for after the workshop. It assumes you worked through the Track B Agent extension callouts and want to use a coding agent on your own R or Python projects. The examples use Claude Code and the ml103-penguins/ project, but the habits apply to any coding agent.
Official documentation:
Commands and keys change between versions. If something here does not match what you see, the official docs win.
crumbs: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code

title: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code
section: 1. Run Claude Code Inside Your RStudio Project
text:
1. Run Claude Code Inside Your RStudio Project
Claude Code runs in a terminal and works on the folder you start it in. Starting it from your RStudio Project keeps its view of files the same as yours.

Install Claude Code by following the overview page.
Open ml103-penguins.Rproj in RStudio.
Open a terminal tab: Tools > Terminal > New Terminal. RStudio starts it in the project folder.
Run claude. Sign in when it asks.

You now have RStudio’s editor, console and Viewer on one side and the agent in the Terminal tab. When the agent edits a file, RStudio reloads it, so you can read every change in the editor you already know.
Python learners: open the ml103-penguins/ folder in VS Code (or a terminal next to Jupyter), activate the venv with source .venv/bin/activate, then run claude from that folder. Starting the agent with .venv active means python and pip point at the project’s environment, not your system Python.






Warning



The agent reads files in this folder and sends their contents to an offshore provider. Keep only data you could publish in the project folder. Never point an agent at Māori data, health or personal data, ethics-restricted data or commercial data unless your data agreement and your institution explicitly allow it.
crumbs: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code

title: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code
section: 2. Give the Project a Memory File
text:
2. Give the Project a Memory File
Each session starts with no memory of the last one. A project memory file fixes that. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md from the project folder at the start of every session. Many other agents read AGENTS.md instead.
A practical pattern:

Put the rules in AGENTS.md, so any agent can use them.
Make CLAUDE.md short: one line, @AGENTS.md, which imports the rules, plus facts only Claude Code needs.

Examples for this workshop: AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md. Copy both into ml103-penguins/ and edit them.
The /init command asks Claude Code to read the project and draft a CLAUDE.md. Treat the draft as a starting point. Delete anything vague and add the rules that matter to you: the code style, which files it may touch, and what to do before it claims success. Keep the file short; every line uses up context in every session. Run /context to see what the agent has loaded.
crumbs: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code

title: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code
text:
3. Approve Actions Yourself
By default Claude Code asks before it edits a file or runs a command. Read each request before you approve it:

File edits: read the diff. Does it change only what you asked for?
Commands: do you know what the command does? Rscript analysis.R (or python analysis.py) is harmless; rm -rf figures/ is not.
Package installs: would you install this package yourself? In Python, check that pip install runs inside .venv, and that the package is also added to requirements.txt.

You can pre-approve safe commands and block risky ones in .claude/settings.json (see the permissions section of the official docs, or run /permissions). The Mahuika page linked above gives a worked example: it allows squeue --me, sacct -j and module; asks for make, sbatch, scancel, rm, find and du (find and du can scan shared filesystems); and denies reading ~/.ssh/ and ~/.bashrc.






Warning



Do not use --dangerously-skip-permissions, auto mode, or any other mode that approves commands for you. On REANNZ systems this breaks the supervision rule. Anywhere else, it hands an agent your account with no checks.
crumbs: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code

title: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code
text:
4. Plan First, Then Edit
For anything bigger than a one-line fix, ask for a plan before any edits. Claude Code has a plan mode for this (press Shift+Tab to cycle modes). In plan mode the agent reads files and proposes steps but changes nothing.
Plan only, do not edit yet. I want analysis.R to save p_bill and p_mass to
figures/ as PNG files. List the files you would change, the code you would add,
and how you will check it worked.
For Python, swap in analysis.py. Read the plan. Correct it if it is wrong (“use ggsave(), not png()”, or “use fig.savefig(), not plt.show()”) and only then let it make the edits. Fixing a plan costs far less than unpicking a wrong edit.
crumbs: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code

title: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code
text:
5. Give Acceptance Criteria
An agent stops when it believes it has finished. Tell it what “finished” means in terms it can check:
Add a summary table of body mass by species and sex to penguins_report.qmd.

Done means:
- the table uses penguins_clean, not penguins
- it shows n, mean and sd, rounded to 1 decimal place
- `quarto render penguins_report.qmd` finishes with no errors or warnings
- you show me the rendered table's first rows from the HTML or the R output
For the Python report, the same criteria apply with “the R output” replaced by “the Python output”; also require that quarto check jupyter finds .venv.
Each criterion is something you can confirm yourself in under a minute.
crumbs: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code

title: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code
section: 6. Make the Agent Run and Check Its Own Work
text:
6. Make the Agent Run and Check Its Own Work
The rule “always run the code before you claim success” catches most agent mistakes: misspelt columns, missing packages and code that was never executed. Put it in AGENTS.md, and ask for evidence:

“Run Rscript analysis.R and show me the last 20 lines of output.”
“Render the report and tell me the size of the HTML file and any warnings.”
“Check that nrow(penguins_clean) is 333 and show me the output.”
Python: “Run python analysis.py, check that len(penguins_clean) is 333 and show me the output.”

Evidence from a command is not the same as correctness. A plot can render and still show the wrong variable. You still open the HTML and look.
crumbs: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code

title: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code
text:
7. Review the Diff
Before you accept a change, see exactly what changed. In RStudio, the Git pane shows a diff for each file. In the terminal, git diff does the same. Look for:

changes to files you did not ask about
deleted code or comments
new packages in library() calls (Python: import lines and requirements.txt)
hard-coded paths, especially to someone else’s home folder
crumbs: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code

title: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code
text:
8. Use Git Commits as Checkpoints
Commit before you hand the agent a task, and again when you accept the result. If the agent makes a mess, you can return to the last good state with git restore <file> or git checkout -- <file>.
Before you start, show me `git status`. If there are uncommitted changes, stop and
ask me what to do.
Write the commit messages yourself, or read the agent’s suggested message before you accept it. Record AI help in the message if your group expects that (for example, “Summary table drafted with Claude Code, checked by hand”).
crumbs: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code

title: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code
text:
9. On REANNZ Systems
REANNZ has rules for AI agents on Mahuika. Episode 02 covers them; the practical steps are:

Install the REANNZ rules and skills once: /opt/nesi/share/mahuika-agents/install.sh --skills. This links ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md to the REANNZ rules (or adds an import line to your existing file). Run /context in Claude Code to check the rules loaded.
Stay supervised. Run one session at a time, watch it, and quit Claude Code before you log out. Using tmux so a dropped connection does not kill the session is fine while you are there; leaving an agent running in tmux or under nohup after you log out is unsupervised and needs a service account.
No independent access. Never give an agent passwords, SSH keys or tokens.
No inbound tunnels or remote control (for example /remote-control).
Limit scope and load. Your own jobs and files only. Heavy work goes in Slurm jobs, not on the login node. No polling loops: check a job with squeue --me once, with minutes between checks, or chain jobs with sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid>.
You choose the project and approve every sbatch. The agent asks which project code to charge; it never guesses.
Check generated commands against the docs. The REANNZ docs index for AI tools is https://docs.nesi.org.nz/llms.txt.

REANNZ does not support third-party AI tools. If the agent gets something wrong, REANNZ support can help with the cluster, not with the agent.
crumbs: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code

title: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code
text:
A Session Checklist

Commit, or check git status is clean.
Start claude in the project folder. Check /context shows your rules.
Ask for a plan. Correct it.
Give the task with acceptance criteria.
Approve or refuse each action after reading it.
Ask for evidence that it ran: output, row counts, render log.
Read the diff. Open the output yourself.
Commit with a message you wrote or checked.
Quit the agent before you walk away.
crumbs: Agent Track: Going Further with Claude Code

title: Slurm Prompts (Episode 09)
text:
Review a Script
Weak:
is this slurm script ok?
<paste the script>
Better:
Review this Slurm job script for the REANNZ Mahuika cluster. It runs a small
R script (analysis.R) that takes about 2 minutes on 1 CPU, needs under 1 GB of
memory and uses no GPU.

Scheduler facts for this cluster:
- Jobs must be charged to a project with --account (mine is nesi99999).
- No --partition is needed; the scheduler picks one. Only hugemem is requested by name.
- GPUs are requested with --gpus-per-node=<type>:<n>, but this job needs none.
- R is loaded with an environment module named like R/<version>-foss-<year>.
  Do not guess a version; write R/<version> and tell me to check `module spider R`.
- There is no conda environment for this job; R packages are in my user library.
- Slurm does not create output directories.

Return a table with columns: line number, problem, fix. Include missing lines
(use "missing" as the line number). Then give the corrected script.
Do not invent module versions, partitions or paths. List any assumptions you made.

<paste the script>

title: Slurm Prompts (Episode 09)
text:
Write Job Scripts
Weak:
write a slurm script for my R code
Better:
Write two Slurm batch scripts for the REANNZ Mahuika cluster.

Job 1 runs `Rscript analysis.R`. Job 2 runs `quarto render penguins_report.qmd`
to HTML. Both run from my project folder ml103-penguins/ (the folder I submit from).

Cluster facts:
- Account: --account=nesi99999 (placeholder, I will replace it).
- No --partition (the scheduler chooses). No GPU.
- Size: 1 CPU, 2 GB memory, 15 minutes for job 1; 1 CPU, 4 GB, 20 minutes for job 2.
- Load R with `module purge` then `module load R/<version>`; do not guess the version.
  Tell me to check it with `module spider R`.
- I do not know if Quarto is a module. Write a commented line for it and tell me
  how to check (`module spider quarto`). Make the job stop with a clear error if
  the quarto command is missing.
- Run R with `srun Rscript`.
- cd to $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR. Write stdout to logs/%x_%j.out and stderr to
  logs/%x_%j.err, and remind me that Slurm does not create logs/.
- R packages are already installed; do not install anything in the job.

Use `#!/bin/bash -e`. Comment each #SBATCH line. List anything you assumed.

Check a Module Name
You suggested `module load <name>`. I ran `module spider <software>` on the
cluster and got this output:
<paste output>
Which exact module name should the script load? Do not suggest a name that is

text: Copy-paste prompts from the R episodes 04 to 08. Each pair shows the quick version a learner might type and a better version. Replace anything in <angle brackets> and 4.x with your own details before you send it.

title: R Prompt Library
text:
04. Load and Explore
Episode: r/04-explore.md

Explore the Data
Quick version
analyse the penguins data in R
Better version
I am using R 4.x in RStudio with the tidyverse and the palmerpenguins package.
I ran library(tidyverse), library(palmerpenguins) and glimpse(penguins).
This is the output:

<paste your glimpse(penguins) output here>

Using only the column names shown above, write R code that:
1. counts the penguins of each species
2. counts the missing values in every column

Use tidyverse functions and the native pipe |>. Do not use other packages.
Give the complete code in one block, then explain each line in one sentence.

title: R Prompt Library
text:
05. Wrangle with dplyr and Debug
Episode: r/05-wrangle.md

Clean and Summarise
Quick version
clean the penguins data and summarise it
Better version
I am using R 4.x with the tidyverse and palmerpenguins. The data frame is
`penguins` with these columns:
<paste your glimpse(penguins) output here>

Write tidyverse code with the native pipe |> that:
1. creates penguins_clean: remove only the rows where sex is NA, then add a
   column body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000
2. creates species_summary: for each species, the number of penguins (n) and
   the mean and standard deviation of bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm and
   body_mass_g. Use .groups = "drop".

Use filter(), mutate(), group_by() and summarise(). Do not use drop_na(),
na.omit() or na.rm = TRUE: penguins_clean should have no missing values left.
After the code, give me base R lines (nrow, table, tapply) that I can use to
check the results.


Debug with an AI
Quick version
my R code doesn't work
Better version
I am using R 4.x with dplyr (from the tidyverse) and palmerpenguins.
This code:

males <- penguins_clean |>
  filter(sex = "male")

gives this error:

Error in filter(penguins_clean, sex = "male") : We detected a named input.
ℹ This usually means that you've used `=` instead of `==`.
ℹ Did you mean `sex == "male"`?

Relevant lines from sessionInfo():
R version 4.x.x ...
other attached packages: dplyr_1.x.x ...

penguins_clean has 333 rows and a factor column sex with levels female and
male. I expected a data frame of the male penguins only.
Explain the cause in one or two sentences and give me the corrected line.
Do not change anything else.

title: R Prompt Library
text:
06. Visualise with ggplot2
Episode: r/06-visualise.md

Bill Length vs Bill Depth
Quick version
plot penguins in ggplot
Better version
I am using R 4.x with ggplot2 4.x (tidyverse) and the data frame
penguins_clean (palmerpenguins columns, no missing values).

Write ggplot2 code that creates an object called p_bill:
- x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, points coloured by species
- one straight-line fit per species: geom_smooth(method = "lm",
  formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE), using linewidth not size
- a colour-blind-safe palette (scale_colour_viridis_d)
- axis labels with units: "Bill length (mm)", "Bill depth (mm)"; legend title "Species"
- theme_minimal()
Then print p_bill and save it with
ggsave("figures/bill_length_depth.png", p_bill, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300),
creating the figures folder if it does not exist.
Give the complete code in one block.


Body Mass by Species and Sex
Quick version
make a boxplot of penguin weight
Better version
Using penguins_clean (palmerpenguins columns) and ggplot2, create p_mass:
body_mass_g by species as a boxplot (outlier.shape = NA) with the individual
penguins as jittered points (width = 0.2, height = 0), one panel per sex
(facet_wrap), boxes filled by species with scale_fill_viridis_d, y label
"Body mass (g)", no x label, no legend, theme_minimal().
Save it with ggsave("figures/body_mass.png", p_mass, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300).

title: R Prompt Library
text:
07. Statistics
Episode: r/07-statistics.md

Bill Length and Bill Depth
Quick version
Is there a relationship between bill length and bill depth in penguins? Give me R code.
Better version
I am using R with the tidyverse and the data frame penguins_clean
(palmerpenguins columns). The data contain three species.

I want to know how bill_depth_mm relates to bill_length_mm.
1. Fit the relationship for all penguins together, then separately within
   each species, using lm() and the native pipe |>.
2. Tell me whether the two answers could disagree, and why.
3. List the variables in this dataset that could confound the relationship.
Do not state a conclusion until I have run the code.


Body Mass by Species
Quick version
what does this mean?
<pasted summary(mass_model) output>
Better version
I fitted lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_clean) in R, where species
is a factor with levels Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo. Here is summary() output:

<paste summary(mass_model) output>

Explain each part of the output (Call, Residuals, each Coefficients row and
column, Residual standard error, R-squared, F-statistic) in plain language for
a biologist. Say which species is the reference level and what the intercept
means. List the assumptions of this model and what would make the conclusions
wrong. Finish with one claim from your explanation that I can check myself in
base R, and the code to check it.


t-Test Check
Write R code for a t-test of whether male and female penguins differ in body
mass, and tell me when this test would be wrong.


Review-Only Second Opinion
Paste your code into a fresh chat (or a different AI assistant) first.
Review this code only. Do not change it. List any errors, and the
assumptions this analysis makes.

title: R Prompt Library
text:
08. Assemble the Quarto Report
Episode: r/08-report.md

Build the Report
Quick version
write a report about the penguins data
Better version
I have an R script analysis.R (tidyverse, palmerpenguins, native pipe |>) that
creates penguins_clean, species_summary, p_bill, p_mass and
mass_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_clean).
Here is the script:

<paste analysis.R>

Turn it into a Quarto document penguins_report.qmd that renders to HTML with
`quarto render penguins_report.qmd`.
- YAML header: title, author, date: today, format: html with
  embed-resources: true, code-fold: true and toc: true
- A setup chunk that loads the packages (message: false)
- Sections: Introduction and data source; Data cleaning; Summary tables
  (by species, island and sex, using knitr::kable); Figures; Simple comparison
  (overall vs per-species slopes, mass_model); Limitations; AI-use statement;
  Session information (sessionInfo())
- Use Quarto #| chunk options with labels, figure captions and fig-width: 7,
  fig-height: 5

title: 08. Assemble the Quarto Report
text:
What a Quarto Report Is
A Quarto document (.qmd) mixes text written in Markdown with Python code cells. The line jupyter: python3 in its header tells Quarto to use the Jupyter engine. When you render it, Quarto starts a fresh Python kernel, runs every cell from top to bottom and writes an HTML file with your text, code, tables and figures. Variables from your terminal or VS Code session do not exist in that kernel, so the report must import the packages and create every object itself.
Quarto has to find the Python that has your packages. Activate the .venv environment before you render (source .venv/bin/activate, or .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows) and run quarto check jupyter. It should report the Python inside .venv. If it reports another one, set the QUARTO_PYTHON environment variable to the full path of .venv’s Python.
In VS Code, install the Quarto extension, then create a new file and save it as penguins_report.qmd in your project folder.

These notes use seaborn’s classic functions (sns.scatterplot(), sns.regplot(), sns.boxplot(), sns.stripplot()) on matplotlib figures, because that is what most AI answers produce. p_bill and p_mass are matplotlib Figure objects.

Prompt 1: the quick version

Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

The AI picks the question. You may get sns.pairplot() of every column, or a bar chart of species counts, which is a valid plot but not the one you need.
One trend line for all species. sns.regplot() has no hue argument. sns.regplot(..., hue="species") stops with TypeError: regplot() got an unexpected keyword argument 'hue', and the usual “fix” drops hue, which fits one line through all the penguins. That line slopes the wrong way (episode 07 explains why).
A figure-level function in an axes-level layout. sns.lmplot(hue="species") does draw one line per species, but it makes its own figure (a FacetGrid). It has no ax= argument and ignores plt.subplots(figsize=...); its size comes from height= and aspect=. Mixing the two families gives empty figures or the wrong size.
Outdated arguments. seaborn 0.12 replaced ci= with errorbar= in barplot(), pointplot() and lineplot(). Old code still draws, with a warning: FutureWarning: The `ci` parameter is deprecated. Use `errorbar='sd'` for the same effect. regplot() and lmplot() still use ci=, so the AI cannot apply one rule everywhere.
Missing values dropped in silence. seaborn leaves out rows with NaN and gives no warning. Plot penguins_clean so the plot and your tables use the same 333 penguins.
Default colours. The default palette includes red and green hues that many people with colour-vision deficiency cannot tell apart.
Axis labels from column names (bill_length_mm) and no units.
Saving the wrong thing. In a script, plt.savefig() after plt.show() saves an empty image once you close the plot window. Without figsize= and dpi=, matplotlib uses its defaults (6.4 × 4.8 inches at 100 dpi), so the file is too small to print.

What typically goes wrong

No question, so no useful answer. “Analyse” can mean anything. AI assistants often return a long tour: describe(), a correlation heatmap, a pair plot and a regression, none of which you asked for or can check in 15 minutes.
The wrong penguins. Many answers load the data with sns.load_dataset("penguins"). That function downloads a CSV file from the seaborn-data repository on GitHub every time the cache is empty, so it fails without internet access, for example on most cluster compute nodes. It also differs from the palmerpenguins package: it has 7 columns (no year) and stores sex as Male and Female, while palmerpenguins uses male and female. Code that tests sex == "male" finds 168 penguins in one and none in the other.
Invented imports. from palmerpenguins import penguins runs without an error, but it imports a module, not a data frame. The next line, penguins.head(), stops with AttributeError: module 'palmerpenguins.penguins' has no attribute 'head'. Other answers read a penguins.csv file that you do not have.
Extra packages. Answers often import ydata-profiling, missingno or plotly, which you have not installed, so the script stops with ModuleNotFoundError.
Silent NA handling. pandas skips missing values in mean(), sum() and value_counts() by default and does not tell you. An answer can report means without saying how many penguins each one used.



Prompt 2: a better version
I am using Python 3.x with pandas 2.x and the palmerpenguins package (pip).
I loaded the data with:

from palmerpenguins import load_penguins
penguins = load_penguins()

penguins.info() gives:

<paste your penguins.info() output here>

Using only the column names shown above, write Python code that:
1. counts the penguins of each species
2. counts the missing values in every column

Use pandas only. Do not use sns.load_dataset() or any other package.
Print each result with print().
Give the complete code in one block, then explain each line in one sentence.







Part of the prompt
What it fixes




Python 3.x with pandas 2.x and the palmerpenguins package
Tells the AI which data source you use and which pandas behaviour to expect


The two lines that load the data
The AI builds on your object name, penguins, not its own


Pasted info() output
Real column names and types, so the AI does not guess them


Using only the column names shown above
Stops the AI inventing columns such as weight


Two numbered, specific questions
Small answers you can check in a minute


Do not use sns.load_dataset()
No second copy of the data with different sex values


explain each line
You read the code before you run it






Example AI output (instructor testing)

Tool: [AI tool, e.g. Google Search AI Mode] · Date tested: [YYYY-MM-DD]
Code returned:
import pandas as pd
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

penguins = load_penguins()

# 1. Count the penguins of each species
species_counts = penguins["species"].value_counts()
print(species_counts)

# 2. Count the missing values in every column
missing_counts = penguins.isna().sum()
print(missing_counts)
Output when run:
species
Adelie       152
Gentoo       124
Chinstrap     68
Name: count, dtype: int64
species               0
island                0
bill_length_mm        2
bill_depth_mm         2
flipper_length_mm     2
body_mass_g           2
sex                  11
year                  0
dtype: int64
Notes: [What worked, what needed fixing, anything worth showing learners]

Replace 3.x and 2.x with your versions. Run python --version in the terminal and print(pd.__version__) in Python. pandas 3 prints text columns in info() as str; pandas 2 prints them as object. Both are fine.


Check it
Run the AI’s code, then check its answers with plain pandas you already know:
print(len(penguins))                       # total rows
print(penguins["species"].value_counts())  # penguins per species
print(len(penguins) - penguins.count())    # missing values per column
count() counts the values that are not missing, so subtracting it from the number of rows gives the missing values without using isna(). You should get 344 rows: 152 Adelie, 68 Chinstrap and 124 Gentoo. Four measurement columns have 2 missing values each and sex has 11. If the AI’s counts differ, find out why before you go on.
The two-penguins trap. Load the seaborn copy next to yours and compare them (this needs internet access):
import seaborn as sns

penguins_sns = sns.load_dataset("penguins")  # downloads a CSV from GitHub
print(penguins.columns.tolist())             # 8 columns, including year
print(penguins_sns.columns.tolist())         # 7 columns, no year
print(penguins["sex"].unique())              # male, female and nan
print(penguins_sns["sex"].unique())          # Male, Female and nan
print(len(penguins_sns.query("sex == 'male'")))  # 0
Both copies hold the same 344 penguins, and the measurement columns have the same names. The differences sit in the details: the missing year column and the capitalised sex values. An AI that learned from seaborn tutorials writes "Male"; one that learned from palmerpenguins writes "male". Neither error message tells you, because a filter that matches nothing returns an empty data frame, not an error.
load_penguins() reads a CSV file that ships inside the palmerpenguins package, so it works offline and on a cluster compute node. Use it for every episode.
Ask your AI assistant: “Which column names does the penguins dataset have, and how is sex coded?” Note whether its answer matches info() and unique().


Reference solution

import pandas as pd
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

penguins = load_penguins()  # palmerpenguins, not sns.load_dataset("penguins")

penguins.info()

# How many penguins of each species?
print(penguins.groupby("species").size())

# How many missing values in each column?
print(penguins.isna().sum())

# Check it with plain pandas
print(len(penguins))                       # 344
print(penguins["species"].value_counts())  # Adelie 152, Gentoo 124, Chinstrap 68
print(len(penguins) - penguins.count())    # 2 in each measurement column, 11 in sex

title: 08. Assemble the Quarto Report
text:
Time: 20 min · Track A (web AI) and Track B (agents)
Questions - How do I turn analysis.R into a report that anyone can re-run? - What goes in an AI-use statement?
Objectives - Create penguins_report.qmd from the code in analysis.R, with a section skeleton you choose. - Render it to a single HTML file with quarto render penguins_report.qmd. - Add a Limitations section, an AI-use statement and sessionInfo().

title: 08. Assemble the Quarto Report
text:
What a Quarto Report Is
A Quarto document (.qmd) mixes text written in Markdown with R code chunks. When you render it, Quarto starts a fresh R session, runs every chunk from top to bottom and writes an HTML file with your text, code, tables and figures. Objects in your RStudio Environment do not exist in that session, so the report must load the packages and create every object itself.
In RStudio: File > New File > Quarto Document, untick “Use visual markdown editor”, and save it as penguins_report.qmd in your project folder.

title: 08. Assemble the Quarto Report
text:
Build the Report

Prompt 1: the quick version
write a report about the penguins data
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

Prose instead of a document. You get an essay about penguins with invented numbers, not a .qmd file that computes them.
R Markdown header in a Quarto file. output: html_document is R Markdown. Quarto uses format: html. Old answers also use self-contained: true, which Quarto replaced with embed-resources: true.
Objects that do not exist at render time. Chunks use penguins_clean or p_bill without creating them, because they existed in your Environment. The render fails with object 'penguins_clean' not found.
Things that should never be in a report: install.packages(), setwd("C:/Users/...") or rm(list = ls()).
Hard-coded numbers in the text (“344 penguins”) that go out of date when the data change. Inline R code, such as `r nrow(penguins)`, keeps them correct.
Old chunk options ({r, echo=FALSE}) mixed with Quarto’s #| options. Both work in Quarto; mixing them makes the file harder to read.



Prompt 2: a better version
I have an R script analysis.R (tidyverse, palmerpenguins, native pipe |>) that
creates penguins_clean, species_summary, p_bill, p_mass and
mass_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_clean).
Here is the script:

<paste analysis.R>

Turn it into a Quarto document penguins_report.qmd that renders to HTML with
`quarto render penguins_report.qmd`.
- YAML header: title, author, date: today, format: html with
  embed-resources: true, code-fold: true and toc: true
- A setup chunk that loads the packages (message: false)
- Sections: Introduction and data source; Data cleaning; Summary tables
  (by species, island and sex, using knitr::kable); Figures; Simple comparison
  (overall vs per-species slopes, mass_model); Limitations; AI-use statement;
  Session information (sessionInfo())
- Use Quarto #| chunk options with labels, figure captions and fig-width: 7,
  fig-height: 5
- Create every object inside the document. No install.packages(), setwd() or
  rm(list = ls()).
- Use inline R code for every number in the text.
Leave the Limitations and AI-use statement sections as headings with a
placeholder sentence: I will write those myself.







Part of the prompt
What it fixes




Pasted analysis.R and the object names
The AI reuses your checked code, not new code


quarto render penguins_report.qmd and format: html
A Quarto file, not R Markdown


embed-resources: true
One HTML file you can email or upload, with figures inside it


code-fold: true
Readers see results first; code is one click away


The section list
Your report structure, not the AI’s


Create every object inside the document
The report renders in a fresh session


inline R code for every number
Numbers in the text match the data


I will write those myself
The judgement sections stay yours






Example AI output (instructor testing)

Code returned:
---

author: "Your Name"
date: today
format:

  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>

leaving `r nrow(penguins_clean)` penguins.

*I will write this section myself.*

  document-css: false
  link-citations: true
  date-format: long
  lang: en

  author: Your Name

Output created: penguins_report.html
Notes: Rendered first time with no errors and no penguins_report_files/ folder. Shortened here: the full answer also had Summary tables, Figures and Simple comparison sections.



Write the Limitations and AI-use statement yourself
Limitations. Use what you found in episode 07. At minimum: the data are observational; species and island are confounded (Chinstrap only on Dream, Gentoo only on Biscoe); the body mass model ignores sex; which rows you removed and why; which assumptions you did not check. If you left out an analysis because you could not explain it, say so here.
Also ask: could more data change this conclusion, or is it variation that more data would not remove (Carpentries: FAIR explainable ML)?
Describe the data. Datasheets and model cards (Carpentries: FAIR explainable ML) ask the same four things your report should answer:

Where the data came from (citation and licence)
Who or what it covers, and what it leaves out
Which rows you removed, and why
Known biases or gaps

AI-use statement. Use the statement you drafted in episode 01:
Generative AI tools were used in this analysis. [Tool name and version, and
date accessed] was used to [task, for example: draft R code for data cleaning,
summary tables, figures and the linear model]. All AI-generated code was run,
read and checked against [method, for example: base R results and row counts]
by the author, who takes responsibility for the final content. Prompts used
are recorded in [file or appendix]. No sensitive or identifiable data was
entered into any AI tool.
If you used an agent (Track B), add one sentence:
An AI agent ([tool name and version]) read files, edited code and ran commands
in the project folder; the author approved each action.
Edit it so it is true for you: name the actual tool, version and date, and list what you actually used it for.


Render it
In the RStudio Terminal (not the Console), from your project folder:
quarto render penguins_report.qmd
Or click Render in RStudio. Quarto writes penguins_report.html next to the .qmd. Open it in your browser.






Note



R Markdown fallback. If Quarto is not installed, save the file as penguins_report.Rmd, change the header to output: html_document with self_contained: true and code_folding: hide, replace date: today with date: "`r Sys.Date()`", and render with rmarkdown::render("penguins_report.Rmd") in the Console. The chunks and text stay the same. Remove the @fig- cross-references, which R Markdown does not support.




Check it

Fresh session. Restart R (Session > Restart R), clear the Environment and render again. If it still renders, the report does not depend on objects you created by hand.
Numbers match. The Data cleaning section should say 11 rows removed and 333 rows left. The species table should match species_summary from analysis.R. The Simple comparison should report an overall slope of −0.082.
One file. There should be no penguins_report_files/ folder next to the HTML. If there is, embed-resources: true is missing or mis-indented.
Every section present, including Limitations, the AI-use statement and the sessionInfo() output at the end.
Read your Limitations aloud. Can you explain every number and model in the report? If not, take it out or say why it is uncertain.

The full reference report is in solutions/penguins_report.qmd (also checkpoints/after-08.qmd). Its header and the start of the body:

title: 06. Visualise with ggplot2
text:
Time: 20 min · Track A (web AI) and Track B (agents)
Questions - What does a plot prompt need so the first answer is close to publishable? - How do I check that a plot shows all the data and the right relationship?
Objectives - Create p_bill and p_mass with prompts that name the variables, mappings, palette, labels and output size. - Recognise outdated ggplot2 code (size = for lines) from its warning. - Check a plot by counting its points and comparing it with a quick base R plot. - Save figures to figures/ with ggsave().

title: 06. Visualise with ggplot2
text:
Bill Length vs Bill Depth

Prompt 1: the quick version
plot penguins in ggplot
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

The AI picks the question. You may get a bar chart of species counts or flipper length against body mass, which is a valid plot but not the one you need.
One trend line for all species. If colour = species sits only inside geom_point(), geom_smooth() fits one line through all the penguins. That line slopes the wrong way (episode 07 explains why).
Outdated arguments. geom_smooth(size = 1) and geom_line(size = 1) come from ggplot2 before 3.4.0. They still draw, with a warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0. Please use `linewidth` instead. Points still use size.
Missing values. Plotting raw penguins gives the warning Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). Plot penguins_clean instead.
Default colours. The default red, green and blue hues are hard to tell apart for many people with colour-vision deficiency.
Axis labels from column names (bill_length_mm) and no units.
ggsave() without a size, so the file takes the size of your plot window and changes every time you resize RStudio.



Prompt 2: a better version
I am using R 4.x with ggplot2 4.x (tidyverse) and the data frame
penguins_clean (palmerpenguins columns, no missing values).

Write ggplot2 code that creates an object called p_bill:
- x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, points coloured by species
- one straight-line fit per species: geom_smooth(method = "lm",
  formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE), using linewidth not size
- a colour-blind-safe palette (scale_colour_viridis_d)
- axis labels with units: "Bill length (mm)", "Bill depth (mm)"; legend title "Species"
- theme_minimal()
Then print p_bill and save it with
ggsave("figures/bill_length_depth.png", p_bill, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300),
creating the figures folder if it does not exist.
Give the complete code in one block.







Part of the prompt
What it fixes




ggplot2 4.x and linewidth not size
Current argument names, no deprecation warning


penguins_clean
No missing-value warning; same rows as your tables


Exact x, y and colour mapping
The plot you need, with one line per species


scale_colour_viridis_d
Colours most readers can tell apart, also in greyscale


Labels with units
A figure readers understand without the code


ggsave(… width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)
The same file every time you run the script


object called p_bill
The report in episode 08 reuses this name






Example AI output (instructor testing)

Tool: [AI tool, e.g. Google Search AI Mode] · Date tested: [YYYY-MM-DD]
Code returned:
p_bill <- ggplot(penguins_clean,
                 aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d() +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)", colour = "Species") +
  theme_minimal()

print(p_bill)

if (!dir.exists("figures")) dir.create("figures")
ggsave("figures/bill_length_depth.png", p_bill, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)
Output when run:
[plot: figures/bill_length_depth.png]
Notes: No warnings. Each species’ line slopes upwards. The default viridis palette ends in pale yellow, which is hard to see on white; the reference uses end = 0.85.

Find your ggplot2 version with packageVersion("ggplot2").


Check it
Predict first. Before you run the AI’s code, say or sketch what the plot should show (for example, three species clusters, or Gentoo heaviest in the body mass plot), then compare (Carpentries: coding with LLMs).
A plot can look right and still be wrong. Check three things:
nrow(layer_data(p_bill, 1))   # points drawn: should be 333, nrow(penguins_clean)
plot(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = penguins_clean,
     col = penguins_clean$species)  # quick base R version of the same plot
file.exists("figures/bill_length_depth.png")
Compare the two plots. Both should show three clusters. In the ggplot2 version, each species’ line should slope upwards. If you see a single downward line, the colour mapping is in the wrong place.


Reference solution

p_bill <- ggplot(
  penguins_clean,
  aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.85) +
  labs(
    x = "Bill length (mm)",
    y = "Bill depth (mm)",
    colour = "Species",
    title = "Bill depth increases with bill length within each species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p_bill

dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave("figures/bill_length_depth.png", p_bill, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)

title: 06. Visualise with ggplot2
section: Body Mass by Species and Sex
text:
Body Mass by Species and Sex

Prompt 1: the quick version
make a boxplot of penguin weight
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

Points drawn twice. A boxplot draws outliers as points; adding geom_jitter() draws them a second time. Use outlier.shape = NA.
Jitter in both directions. By default geom_jitter() moves points up and down as well as sideways, so points no longer sit at their true body mass. Set height = 0 to keep the values true and spread points sideways only.
Sex left out, although males are heavier in every species.
weight invented as a column name. The column is body_mass_g.



Prompt 2: a better version
Using penguins_clean (palmerpenguins columns) and ggplot2, create p_mass:
body_mass_g by species as a boxplot (outlier.shape = NA) with the individual
penguins as jittered points (width = 0.2, height = 0), one panel per sex
(facet_wrap), boxes filled by species with scale_fill_viridis_d, y label
"Body mass (g)", no x label, no legend, theme_minimal().
Save it with ggsave("figures/body_mass.png", p_mass, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300).







Part of the prompt
What it fixes




body_mass_g
No invented weight column


outlier.shape = NA
Each penguin drawn once


height = 0
Jitter moves points sideways only, so masses stay true


one panel per sex
Shows the sex difference the model in episode 07 ignores






Example AI output (instructor testing)

Tool: [AI tool, e.g. Google Search AI Mode] · Date tested: [YYYY-MM-DD]
Code returned:

  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_mass

ggsave("figures/body_mass.png", p_mass, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)
Output when run:
[plot: figures/body_mass.png]
Notes: No warnings. Check the jitter has height = 0 so masses are not moved.



Check it
nrow(layer_data(p_mass, 2))                          # jittered points: 333
tapply(penguins_clean$body_mass_g,
       list(penguins_clean$species, penguins_clean$sex), median)
The medians from tapply() should match the thick line in each box.


Reference solution

p_mass <- ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~sex) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.85) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)", title = "Body mass by species and sex") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_mass

ggsave("figures/body_mass.png", p_mass, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)

text:
Time: 15 min · Track A (web AI) and Track B (agents)
Questions - How do I give an AI assistant enough context to write code for my data? - How do I know the AI used the right dataset and the right column names?
Objectives - Load the tidyverse and palmerpenguins in a fresh R session. - Paste glimpse() output into a prompt so the AI sees the real column names. - Check AI-written exploration code against base R (nrow(), table(), is.na()). - Explain why R 4.5 and later has two different penguins datasets.

title: 04. Load and Explore the Penguins
text:
Set Up the Script
Open your ml103-penguins RStudio Project and create a new script called analysis.R. You will add to this one script in episodes 04 to 07. Start it with two lines and run them:
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
Then run glimpse(penguins) and keep the output on screen. You will paste it into your prompt.






Warning



Paste code, error messages and glimpse() output into a web AI. Do not paste real research data. The penguins data are public, which is why we use them.

title: 04. Load and Explore the Penguins
text:
Explore the Data

Prompt 1: the quick version
analyse the penguins data in R
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

No question, so no useful answer. “Analyse” can mean anything. AI assistants often return a long tour: a summary, a correlation matrix, three plots and a regression, none of which you asked for or can check in 15 minutes.
The wrong penguins. Since R 4.5.0, base R ships its own penguins in the datasets package with short column names (bill_len, bill_dep, flipper_len, body_mass). The palmerpenguins package uses bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm and body_mass_g. The AI cannot see which one you have, so it may mix the two sets of names in one script.
Missing library() calls. Code that uses glimpse() or count() without library(tidyverse) stops with could not find function "glimpse".
Mixed styles. Base R, %>% and |> in the same answer, or functions from packages you have not installed (skimr, GGally, janitor).
Silent NA handling. Means and correlations computed with na.rm = TRUE without saying so, or NA results that the answer does not mention.



Prompt 2: a better version
I am using R 4.x in RStudio with the tidyverse and the palmerpenguins package.
I ran library(tidyverse), library(palmerpenguins) and glimpse(penguins).
This is the output:

<paste your glimpse(penguins) output here>

Using only the column names shown above, write R code that:
1. counts the penguins of each species
2. counts the missing values in every column

Use tidyverse functions and the native pipe |>. Do not use other packages.
Give the complete code in one block, then explain each line in one sentence.







Part of the prompt
What it fixes




R 4.x … tidyverse and the palmerpenguins package
Tells the AI which penguins you mean and which style to write


Pasted glimpse() output
Real column names and types, so the AI does not guess them


Using only the column names shown above
Stops the AI switching to bill_len or inventing columns


Two numbered, specific questions
Small answers you can check in a minute


native pipe |> and no other packages
Consistent style that runs on your setup


explain each line
You read the code before you run it






Example AI output (instructor testing)

Tool: [AI tool, e.g. Google Search AI Mode] · Date tested: [YYYY-MM-DD]
Code returned:
# 1. Count the penguins of each species
penguins |>
  count(species)

# 2. Count the missing values in every column
penguins |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x))))
Output when run:
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species       n
  <fct>     <int>
1 Adelie      152
2 Chinstrap    68
3 Gentoo      124
# A tibble: 1 × 8
  species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g
    <int>  <int>          <int>         <int>             <int>       <int>
1       0      0              2             2                 2           2
# ℹ 2 more variables: sex <int>, year <int>
Notes: Counts match the base R check (152, 68, 124; 2 NAs per measurement column, 11 in sex). The AI used ~ sum(is.na(.x)) rather than \(x); both work.

Replace 4.x with your version (run R.version.string).


Check it
Run the AI’s code, then check its answers with base R you already know:
nrow(penguins)            # total rows
table(penguins$species)   # penguins per species
colSums(is.na(penguins))  # missing values per column
You should get 344 rows: 152 Adelie, 68 Chinstrap and 124 Gentoo. Four measurement columns have 2 missing values each and sex has 11. If the AI’s counts differ, find out why before you go on.
The two-penguins trap. On R 4.5 or later, restart R (Session > Restart R) and run this before loading palmerpenguins:
names(penguins)                  # base R version: bill_len, bill_dep, ...
library(palmerpenguins)
names(penguins)                  # now: bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, ...
names(datasets::penguins)        # base R version, by its full name
names(palmerpenguins::penguins)  # package version, by its full name
When you load palmerpenguins, R prints that penguins and penguins_raw are masked from package:datasets. From then on, penguins means the package version. The order matters: if your script uses bill_length_mm but you forgot library(palmerpenguins), R 4.5 finds the base R penguins instead and you get errors such as Column `bill_length_mm` doesn't exist. Worse, base R code like mean(penguins$bill_length_mm) returns NA with only a warning. Code written with bill_len runs only on R 4.5 or later and fails on R 4.3 and 4.4. The two datasets hold the same 344 penguins, so the numbers agree once the names match.
On R 4.3 or 4.4, the first names(penguins) gives an “object not found” error, because base R has no penguins yet.
Ask your AI assistant: “Which column names does the penguins dataset have?” Note whether its answer matches glimpse().


Reference solution

library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins) # load AFTER tidyverse; masks datasets::penguins on R >= 4.5

glimpse(penguins)

# How many penguins of each species?
penguins |>
  count(species)

# How many missing values in each column?
penguins |>
  summarise(across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x))))

# Check it with base R
nrow(penguins)              # 344
table(penguins$species)     # Adelie 152, Chinstrap 68, Gentoo 124
colSums(is.na(penguins))    # 2 in each measurement column, 11 in sex
Catch-up file: checkpoints/after-04.R.







Tip



Agent extension (Track B) Give the agent the task with acceptance criteria instead of pasting output:
Create analysis.R in this project. It must start with library(tidyverse)
then library(palmerpenguins), use the native pipe |>, count penguins per
species and count missing values per column. Run it with Rscript and show me
the output. Acceptance: 344 rows; species counts match table(penguins$species);
the script uses only palmerpenguins column names (bill_length_mm, not bill_len).
Approve each file edit and each Rscript run. Then ask the agent to check which penguins the script uses with find("penguins") and to explain the result.

title: 09. AI for Slurm Scripts: Review and Write
section: Mahuika Facts Used in This Episode
text:
Mahuika Facts Used in This Episode
An AI assistant has no way to know these facts about your cluster unless you tell it. Each one below comes from the REANNZ docs (checked October 2026).



Fact
Source




Charge jobs to a project with --account. The docs use nesi99999 as the example code. You can leave it out only if you belong to a single project.
Batch Computing Guide, Slurm reference sheet


No --partition needed. Mahuika chooses one automatically. Only hugemem must be requested by name.
Mahuika HPC3 differences


GPUs are requested with --gpus-per-node=<type>:<n> (types a100, h100, l4, pro_6000).
Using GPUs


R modules are named like R/4.6.0-foss-2026. Find them with module spider R (ignores case) or module avail (case-sensitive).
Environment and modules, R


The R examples run scripts with srun Rscript script.R.
R


Python modules are named like Python/3.14.4-foss-2026. The docs recommend a virtual environment for your packages, activated in the job script.
Python


File systems: /home/<username>, /nesi/project/<code>, /nesi/nobackup/<code>.
Filesystems and quotas


Check your own jobs with squeue --me. Plain squeue lists every user’s jobs.
Batch Computing Guide


The REANNZ docs do not list a Quarto module. Check with module spider quarto before you rely on one.
docs.nesi.org.nz/llms.txt (no Quarto page)



One fact is general Slurm behaviour: Slurm does not create the folder named in --output or --error. If logs/ does not exist, the job fails and you get no log file to tell you why. Run mkdir -p logs before you submit.

section: Task A: Review a Flawed Script
text:
Task A: Review a Flawed Script
Open slurm/review-me.sl. Someone adapted it from an old GPU training script to run analysis.R. The job takes about two minutes on one CPU.

 2  #SBATCH --job-name=penguins
 3  #SBATCH --partition=gpu_p100
 4  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
 5  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
 6  #SBATCH --mem=32G
 7  #SBATCH --time=24:00:00
 8  #SBATCH --output=logs/penguins_%j.log
 9
10  # Load required modules
11  module load r/4.3
12
13  # Activate environment
14  source activate r-env
15
16  # Set cache directories
17  export TRANSFORMERS_CACHE=$HOME/.cache/huggingface
18  export HF_HOME=$HOME/.cache/huggingface
19
20  # Run the analysis
21  cd /home/jsmith/ml103-penguins
22  Rscript analysis.R

Prompt 1: the quick version
is this slurm script ok?
<paste the script>
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

The AI often says the script “looks good” and suggests small style changes. It checks the script against generic Slurm, not against your cluster.
It may keep --partition=gpu_p100 because the partition name looks plausible. It has no way to know that Mahuika has no such partition.
It rarely notices that the job asks for a GPU, 8 CPUs, 32 GB and 24 hours for a two-minute, single-threaded R script.
It may “fix” the module line by inventing another plausible name, such as module load R/4.3.1, which may not exist on the cluster.
It seldom mentions that Slurm will not create the logs/ folder.
The answer comes as prose, so you cannot easily tick off each problem.



Prompt 2: a better version
Review this Slurm job script for the REANNZ Mahuika cluster. It runs a small
R script (analysis.R) that takes about 2 minutes on 1 CPU, needs under 1 GB of
memory and uses no GPU.

Scheduler facts for this cluster:
- Jobs must be charged to a project with --account (mine is nesi99999).
- No --partition is needed; the scheduler picks one. Only hugemem is requested by name.
- GPUs are requested with --gpus-per-node=<type>:<n>, but this job needs none.
- R is loaded with an environment module named like R/<version>-foss-<year>.
  Do not guess a version; write R/<version> and tell me to check `module spider R`.
- There is no conda environment for this job; R packages are in my user library.
- Slurm does not create output directories.

Return a table with columns: line number, problem, fix. Include missing lines
(use "missing" as the line number). Then give the corrected script.
Do not invent module versions, partitions or paths. List any assumptions you made.







Part of the prompt
What it fixes




“REANNZ Mahuika”, plus the job’s real size
The AI can judge whether 8 CPUs, 32 GB, a GPU and 24 hours make sense


Scheduler facts list
Replaces generic Slurm advice with your cluster’s rules: account, partitions, GPUs


“Do not guess a version… check module spider R”
Stops the AI from inventing a module name and hands the check back to you


“No conda environment”
Flags source activate as left over from the Python script


“Slurm does not create output directories”
Points the AI at a failure that leaves no log behind


Table of line, problem, fix
Gives you a checklist you can verify one row at a time


“List any assumptions”
Shows you which parts of the answer the AI guessed






Example AI output (instructor testing)

Tool: [AI tool, e.g. Google Search AI Mode] · Date tested: [YYYY-MM-DD]
Code returned:
#!/bin/bash -e
#SBATCH --job-name=penguins            # name shown in squeue
#SBATCH --account=nesi99999            # your project code
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1              # analysis.R is single-threaded
#SBATCH --mem=2G                       # needs under 1 GB
#SBATCH --time=00:15:00                # job takes about 2 minutes
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out        # run `mkdir -p logs` first
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x_%j.err

module purge
module load R/VERSION                  # replace VERSION using: module spider R
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
srun Rscript analysis.R
Output when run:
$ bash -n review-fixed.sl && echo "syntax OK"
syntax OK
[paste sbatch --test-only output from the cluster here]
Notes: [What worked, what needed fixing, anything worth showing learners]



Check it
Compare the AI’s table with the answer key below. For each row the AI got wrong or missed, find the fact in the Mahuika facts table or the linked docs page. If you have a Mahuika account, run module spider R and compare the real module names with what the AI suggested.


Reference solution: answer key




Line
Problem
Fix




1
Without -e, the script carries on after a failed command, such as a failed module load.
#!/bin/bash -e


missing
No --account. If you belong to more than one project, Slurm cannot tell which one to charge.
#SBATCH --account=nesi99999 (your project code)


3
gpu_p100 is not a Mahuika partition. Mahuika picks partitions automatically.
Delete the line


4
Requests a GPU that R never uses. The job waits longer in the queue and wastes a scarce GPU. --gres is also not the syntax the Mahuika docs use.
Delete the line


5
8 CPUs for a single-threaded script; 7 sit idle and count against your allocation.
--cpus-per-task=1


6
32 GB for a job that needs under 1 GB.
--mem=2G


7

--time=00:15:00


8
logs/ may not exist, and Slurm will not create it. The job then fails with no log. No separate error file.
Run mkdir -p logs before submitting; add --error=logs/%x_%j.err


missing
No module purge, so modules loaded in your login session leak into the job.
module purge before module load


11
r/4.3 does not match Mahuika’s naming (R/<version>-foss-<year>). The load fails.
module load R/<version>, with the version from module spider R (the docs show R/4.6.0-foss-2026)


14
source activate is old conda syntax copied from the Python script. No conda environment exists, and R does not need one.
Delete the line


17
TRANSFORMERS_CACHE is a Hugging Face (Python) setting, deprecated even there. R ignores it.
Delete the line


18
HF_HOME is also irrelevant to R.
Delete the line


21
Hard-coded home path for another user (jsmith). It breaks for anyone else.
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"


22
Works, but the REANNZ R docs show R run with srun Rscript.
srun Rscript analysis.R



The corrected script is slurm/run_analysis.sl.







Tip



Agent extension (Track B) Ask the agent to review slurm/review-me.sl with the same scheduler facts and to write its table to the chat, not to a file. Acceptance criteria: every row cites a line number; it does not edit review-me.sl; it marks any module version it could not confirm as <version>. If you are on Mahuika, let it run module spider R (approve the command) and update its answer with what it finds.

title: 09. AI for Slurm Scripts: Review and Write
section: Task B: Write Two Job Scripts
text:
Task B: Write Two Job Scripts
Now write two jobs from scratch: one runs Rscript analysis.R, the other runs quarto render penguins_report.qmd. Both run from your ml103-penguins/ folder.

Prompt 1: the quick version
write a slurm script for my R code
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

The AI invents a partition (compute, normal, standard) and module names (module load R, module load r/4.2.0, module load quarto) that look right but may not exist on your cluster.
It leaves out --account, or uses a made-up placeholder you might not notice.
Resources are generic guesses: often 4 or more CPUs, 8 to 16 GB and several hours, whatever the job really needs.
It writes output to a folder that may not exist, or to the default slurm-<jobid>.out with errors mixed in.
It may install packages inside the job (install.packages(...)), which repeats a slow download every run and can fail on compute nodes.
For Quarto, it often forgets that rendering R chunks needs the knitr and rmarkdown packages as well as the Quarto tool.



Prompt 2: a better version
Write two Slurm batch scripts for the REANNZ Mahuika cluster.

Job 1 runs `Rscript analysis.R`. Job 2 runs `quarto render penguins_report.qmd`
to HTML. Both run from my project folder ml103-penguins/ (the folder I submit from).

Cluster facts:
- Account: --account=nesi99999 (placeholder, I will replace it).
- No --partition (the scheduler chooses). No GPU.
- Size: 1 CPU, 2 GB memory, 15 minutes for job 1; 1 CPU, 4 GB, 20 minutes for job 2.
- Load R with `module purge` then `module load R/<version>`; do not guess the version.
  Tell me to check it with `module spider R`.
- I do not know if Quarto is a module. Write a commented line for it and tell me
  how to check (`module spider quarto`). Make the job stop with a clear error if
  the quarto command is missing.
- Run R with `srun Rscript`.
- cd to $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR. Write stdout to logs/%x_%j.out and stderr to
  logs/%x_%j.err, and remind me that Slurm does not create logs/.
- R packages are already installed; do not install anything in the job.

Use `#!/bin/bash -e`. Comment each #SBATCH line. List anything you assumed.







Part of the prompt
What it fixes




Cluster name and “account placeholder”
The account line is present and obviously yours to replace


“No --partition. No GPU.”
Stops invented partitions and wasted GPU requests


Explicit CPUs, memory and time
Sizes the job for what it does, so it queues quickly


“Do not guess the version… module spider R”
Turns a likely hallucination into a check you run


Quarto check and fail-fast line
Handles a tool you have not confirmed exists


$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR, log paths, logs/ reminder
Fixes the working directory and makes failures visible


“Do not install anything in the job”
Keeps package installs in your interactive session


“List anything you assumed”
Shows what to check before you submit






Example AI output (instructor testing)

Tool: [AI tool, e.g. Google Search AI Mode] · Date tested: [YYYY-MM-DD]
Code returned:
#!/bin/bash -e
#SBATCH --job-name=penguins-analysis   # name shown in squeue
#SBATCH --account=nesi99999            # replace with your project code
#SBATCH --time=00:15:00                # 15 minutes
#SBATCH --mem=2G                       # 2 GB memory
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1              # single-threaded R
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out        # stdout
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x_%j.err         # stderr

module purge
module load R/<version>                # check with: module spider R
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
srun Rscript analysis.R
Output when run:
$ bash -n run_analysis.sl && echo "syntax OK"
run_analysis.sl: line 11: syntax error near unexpected token `newline'
run_analysis.sl: line 11: `module load R/<version>                # check with: module spider R'
[paste sbatch --test-only output from the cluster here]
Notes: [What worked, what needed fixing, anything worth showing learners. Job 1 shown; job 2 (Quarto) omitted. The <version> placeholder is read by bash as a redirect, so bash -n fails until it is replaced with the real module name.]



Check it
AIs invent module names. Check every module load line before you trust it:

Read the docs. Look up the software page, for example R on Mahuika.
Ask the cluster. On a login node, run module spider R and module spider quarto. module spider ignores case; module avail does not. Copy the exact name it prints.
Check the shell syntax. bash -n run_analysis.sl prints nothing if the syntax is valid.
Ask the scheduler. sbatch --test-only run_analysis.sl checks the #SBATCH options against the cluster (account, partition, limits) and estimates a start time. It does not submit the job.
Make the log folder. mkdir -p logs.

Then compare your script with the reference answers.


Reference solution

Full commented versions: slurm/run_analysis.sl and slurm/render_report.sl.

#SBATCH --account=nesi99999            # replace with your project code
#SBATCH --time=00:15:00
#SBATCH --mem=2G
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x_%j.err

module purge

cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
srun Rscript analysis.R
#!/bin/bash -e
#SBATCH --job-name=penguins-report
#SBATCH --account=nesi99999            # replace with your project code
#SBATCH --time=00:20:00
#SBATCH --mem=4G
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x_%j.err

module purge
module load R/4.6.0-foss-2026          # check with: module spider R
# module load Quarto/<version>         # only if `module spider quarto` finds one
command -v quarto >/dev/null || { echo "quarto not found on PATH" >&2; exit 1; }
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
srun quarto render penguins_report.qmd --to html



Python learners
Task A is the same for everyone: review-me.sl runs an R script, and the answer key does not change. For Task B, write the jobs for python analysis.py and the Jupyter engine render of penguins_report.qmd. Adapt Prompt 2 with the differences below. The reference answers are slurm/run_analysis_py.sl and slurm/render_report_py.sl.









R job
Python job




Module
module load R/<version>, from module spider R
module load Python/<version>, from module spider Python (the docs show Python/3.14.4-foss-2026)


Packages
Already in your R user library
In a virtual environment, .venv/ in the project folder. Create it once on a login node with the same module loaded, then source .venv/bin/activate in the job.


Run line
srun Rscript analysis.R
srun python analysis.py


Report render
Quarto plus knitr and rmarkdown
Quarto plus jupyter in the venv. Check with quarto check jupyter.



The AI often adds pip install lines inside the job, or uses conda activate when you have a venv. Both are the same mistake as install.packages() in an R job: install once, interactively, and only activate in the job.






Tip



Agent extension (Track B) Give the agent the same cluster facts and ask it to write slurm/run_analysis.sl and slurm/render_report.sl (Python: run_analysis_py.sl and render_report_py.sl), then check them. Acceptance criteria:

It asks you which project code to charge. It does not guess one.
It runs module spider R (or module spider Python) and uses the exact name it finds.
It runs bash -n and sbatch --test-only on both scripts and shows you the output.
It asks before running sbatch. You approve each submission yourself.

REANNZ agent rules apply on Mahuika. Stay at the keyboard while the agent works. Do not let it poll the queue in a loop (watch squeue, while sleep …). If it needs to check a job, it runs squeue --me once, with minutes between checks, or chains the jobs with sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> so Slurm does the waiting. Running /opt/nesi/share/mahuika-agents/install.sh --skills adds the REANNZ rules and a /mahuika-slurm skill (Claude Code on Mahuika).

title: 02. Rules of the Road: REANNZ Policies for AI Use
text:
Where these rules apply
These rules apply on REANNZ systems, including the Mahuika supercomputer documented at docs.nesi.org.nz. If you work somewhere else, read them as a worked example. Use them to find the questions to ask about your own institution’s acceptable use policy and AI rules.
Two timing points matter:

The agent rules are installed system-wide on Friday 23 October 2026.
From 1 November 2026, REANNZ contacts anyone who is not following them.







Note



Track A learners: when you use a web AI tool in a browser on your own laptop, that tool is not an agent. Data sensitivity and your institution’s acceptable use policy still apply. REANNZ does not support third-party AI tools, so check any command an AI gives you against the documentation before you run it on a REANNZ system.


Read the Acceptable Use Policy and the Access Policy, which sets the conditions for sharing data.

title: 02. Rules of the Road: REANNZ Policies for AI Use
section: You are responsible for every agent action
text:
You are responsible for every agent action
Everything an agent does under your account is your responsibility. Read the rules before you start an agent, not after.

title: 02. Rules of the Road: REANNZ Policies for AI Use
text:
The five rules
Read the official wording on the AI Agent Rules page. In summary:

Agents must be supervised. You start the agent, stay at the session, and approve its actions as they happen. Loops, scheduled tasks, and sessions left running after you log out do not count as supervised.
Agents must not have independent access. An agent must not hold your passwords, SSH keys or tokens, and must not log in by itself. SSH means Secure Shell, the protocol that you use to log in to a remote system.
Agents must not open inbound tunnels. Do not use reverse SSH tunnels, ngrok, VS Code tunnels, or the remote-control features of AI tools. These let connections from outside reach the cluster.
Agents must limit scope and load. Work only on your own jobs and files. Poll the scheduler slowly, use job dependencies instead of polling, and keep heavy work off the login node.
Agents must follow AGENTS.md. This is the REANNZ agent rules file.


Check the scheduler slowly
A login node is shared by every user, so keep checks light. Check your jobs with squeue --me, then wait at least 60 seconds before the next check:
squeue --me
sleep 60
squeue --me
Better still, chain jobs so that the second one starts only when the first finishes successfully. Replace 4018273 with the job ID that sbatch printed for your first job:
sbatch --dependency=afterok:4018273 report.sl
Do not run any of these:







Do not run
Run this instead




watch -n 1 squeue
squeue --me, then sleep 60 between checks


sacct --allusers
sacct -u "$USER" for your own jobs


find /nesi/project or grep -r over /home with no path limit
A named directory, such as grep -r "bill_length" ./analysis


Submitting many jobs to see what works
One test job, check its output, then scale up. sbatch --test-only checks a script without running it


top or ps aux, refreshed without a filter
top -u "$USER" or a single ps -u "$USER"

title: 02. Rules of the Road: REANNZ Policies for AI Use
text:
Is this allowed?
Decide each scenario before you open its answer. Check the answer against the five rules.

Card 1: the overnight session
You start Claude Code in a tmux session on a login node. You close your laptop and leave it running overnight so it can keep submitting jobs.


Answer

Not allowed. Nobody supervises the session once you stop watching or log out. tmux sessions that survive logout need a service account. Stop the session, or wait for a service account.



Card 2: the patient records
A colleague’s dataset has patient ages, postcodes and diagnoses. You paste the first 20 rows into a web chatbot to ask for plot code.


Answer

Not allowed. Health and personal data often cannot leave New Zealand, and web AI tools send your text to an offshore provider. Ask the data owner about an approved route, or practise with openly licensed data such as penguins.



Card 3: the watch loop
Your job is queued, so you run watch -n 1 squeue in a second terminal to see when it starts.


Answer

Not allowed as written. The command checks the scheduler every second and lists every user’s jobs. Run squeue --me, wait 60 seconds with sleep 60, and check again. Or submit the next job with --dependency=afterok: so that it starts by itself.



Card 4: the SSH key
Your agent cannot reach a compute node. It asks you for your SSH key so that it can log in.


Answer

Refuse. Never give an agent your keys, passwords or tokens. Agents must not have independent access. Run the command yourself in your own session, and let the agent read the output.



Card 5: the tunnel
To check a web dashboard from your phone, your agent suggests running ngrok on the login node.


Answer

Not allowed. ngrok is an inbound tunnel, which lets outside connections reach the cluster. Agents must not open inbound tunnels. Ask support for an approved way to view the output.



Card 6: the scratch folder
Your agent offers to clear a scratch folder to free space. The folder contains files you did not create.


Answer

Ask first. The agent must confirm before it deletes files it did not create. List the files yourself, decide what to keep, and approve only the deletions you have checked.



Card 7: the survey columns
You run glimpse() on a Māori community survey and paste the output into Google AI Mode to get plot code.


Answer

Not allowed. Māori data needs care under Te Mana Raraunga and the CARE principles, and web AI tools send your text offshore. glimpse() also prints sample values, not just column names, so check the output before you paste any of it. Practise with penguins instead.



Card 8: the broad search
Your agent runs grep -r "bill" /nesi/project to find a file with your data.


Answer

Not allowed. The search covers every project directory, which is an unscoped search of /nesi/project. Name the directory you expect, such as grep -r "bill" ./analysis.







Tip



Agent extension (Track B) Ask Claude Code to write a short rules check for your planned task. It should list which of the five rules apply and what it will not do. Then open AGENTS.md yourself and read it.
