title: 01. AI and Ethics in Research
section: How a language model writes text
text:
How a language model writes text
A large language model (LLM) predicts the next token, a short chunk of text such as a word or part of a word, from the text that came before it. It does not look up facts, and it does not run your code. A response reads as fluent because the model learned which words usually follow which, not because it checked them.
The model also samples its next token, so the same prompt can give different code each time. Compare your answer with a neighbour’s, and check your own answer rather than copying the instructor’s (adapted from Learning to Code with AI Chatbots).
This explains the most common failure. The model writes a plausible R function even when no such function exists. Researchers call this a hallucination. Three typical forms:

An invented function. For example, penguin_sex_ratio(), which no package exports.
A real function with wrong arguments. For example, a geom_point() call that passes an argument the function does not accept.
A made-up column name. For example, bill_len, when palmerpenguins::penguins (and Python’s load_penguins()) uses bill_length_mm.


Exercise 1: test a made-up function
Ask your AI assistant this question. Do not check the answer before you read the response.
Show me how to use penguin_sex_ratio() from the palmerpenguins package to get the proportion of female penguins for each species. Give me a complete example.
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.
Then check the function yourself.

RPython


In RStudio, run:
library(palmerpenguins)
exists("penguin_sex_ratio")
R returns FALSE. Then run help(package = "palmerpenguins") to see every topic the package documents.


Ask the same question with “Python” in place of “R”, then run:
import palmerpenguins
print(hasattr(palmerpenguins, "penguin_sex_ratio"))
print([name for name in dir(palmerpenguins) if not name.startswith("_")])
The first print() shows False. The second lists everything the package exports, such as load_penguins.



Your AI assistant may still give you a confident example. Note which source you trust more: the AI’s answer or the package’s own index.

title: 01. AI and Ethics in Research
text:
Bias and representativeness
Fluent output is not the same as correct output. The AI reflects patterns in its training data, so it favours common examples and may not notice when your data differs from them.
The penguins data describes 344 penguins from three islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica, collected between 2007 and 2009 (Gorman, Williams and Fraser, 2014). Any result describes these penguins. It does not describe all penguins. Ask yourself what the data cannot tell you before you write a conclusion.
Quick probe (30 seconds). Ask your AI assistant Write one sentence about a typical researcher. Notice who it assumes the researcher is. The same assumptions can leak into code comments and report text, so read those too (adapted from Trustworthy AI).

title: 01. AI and Ethics in Research
text:
Data sovereignty and privacy
Anything you paste into a web AI tool leaves New Zealand. The model runs at an offshore provider. Do not paste the following into a web AI tool:

Māori data, including data about whānau, hapū, iwi or Māori communities. Māori data sovereignty is set out by Te Mana Raraunga and the CARE principles.
Health and personal data, including any record that identifies a person.
Ethics-restricted data, meaning data covered by an approval that limits sharing.
Commercial data, including data under a confidentiality agreement.

Penguins is safe for this workshop because it is openly licensed and describes animals, not people. Before you paste any other data, ask whether the people it describes would expect it to leave New Zealand.

title: 01. AI and Ethics in Research
text:
Research integrity
Research integrity covers three things:

Authorship. An AI tool cannot be an author. You are responsible for every claim in your work.
Disclosure. Say which tool you used and what it did. You write this statement in Exercise 2.
Reproducibility. Record the prompts you used and the package versions you ran. Episode 08 shows how to record versions (R: r/08-report.md, with sessionInfo() · Python: python/08-report.md).

For national guidance, read Royal Society Te Apārangi, Guidelines for the best practice use of GenAI in research (June 2025): PDF. Read its section on disclosure before you finalise your statement.

title: 01. AI and Ethics in Research
text:
Licensing, citation and environmental cost
You own the code you publish, so check every line of generated code before you use it. Terms of use differ between AI providers. Read the terms of the tool you used, and cite the tool and version the way your field or journal asks.
Large models use substantial computing power for each response. Use AI where it saves time on work you can check. Do not use it to skip learning the fundamentals you need to judge its output.

title: 01. AI and Ethics in Research
text:
When not to use AI

When you are learning a skill that you must judge later. Practise first, then use AI to speed up work you already understand.
When the data is sensitive, as described above.
When you cannot check the result. If you cannot tell whether the output is correct, you cannot report it.
When reading feels like learning. An AI explanation can give you an illusion of competence. Type the code, change it, or predict its output yourself (adapted from Learning to Code with AI Chatbots).


Exercise 2: draft an AI-use disclosure statement
Write a statement of two to four sentences that says what you used AI for in this workshop. Start from the template below, then edit it to match what you did. The square brackets mark the parts you fill in.
Generative AI tools were used in this analysis. [Tool name and version, and date accessed] was used to [task, for example: draft R (or Python) code for data cleaning and suggest plot layouts]. All AI-generated code was run, read and checked against [method, for example: base R (or plain pandas) results and row counts] by the author, who takes responsibility for the final content. Prompts used are recorded in [file or appendix]. No sensitive or identifiable data was entered into any AI tool.
If you used an agent (Track B), add one sentence:
An AI agent ([tool name and version]) read files, edited code and ran commands in the project folder; the author approved each action.
Swap statements with a partner. Ask whether a reader could repeat what you did from your statement alone. If not, add the missing detail.






Tip



Agent extension (Track B) Ask the agent to list the files it read and the tasks it did in this session. Compare that list with your disclosure statement, and remove any claim you cannot back up.

title: 01. AI and Ethics in Research
text:
Key points

An LLM predicts plausible text. It does not check facts, so verify every function, argument and column name.
Do not paste Māori, health, ethics-restricted or commercial data into a web AI tool.
Disclose which AI tool you used, what it did, and how you checked the output.
Penguins is safe to use because it is openly licensed and contains no personal data.

title: 03. Anatomy of a Good Prompt
text:
Time: 10 min · Track A (web AI) and Track B (agents)
Questions - What must a prompt say before an AI can write useful R or Python code? - How do you describe your data without pasting it? - How do you make the AI show you how to check its answer?
Objectives - Write a prompt with context, data shape, task, constraints, output format and a verification request. - Use glimpse() output (Python: penguins.info() and penguins.head()) to describe your data. - Use the reusable template at the end of this episode.

title: 03. Anatomy of a Good Prompt
text:
Why the prompt matters
An AI assistant can only use what you give it. If you leave out the R or Python version, the packages, the column names or the style you want, the AI fills the gaps with its own guesses. Those guesses often look right and are not.
Each prompt in this workshop has a weak version and a better version. Write your own attempt first, then compare.

title: 03. Anatomy of a Good Prompt
section: Describe your data without pasting it
text:
Describe your data without pasting it

RPython


Paste the output of glimpse(), not the data. glimpse() shows the column names, their types and a few values. Those sample values are real data, so check them before you paste. For real research data, paste only the column names and types (see Card 7 in episode 02). Run this in RStudio:
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
glimpse(penguins)
The output starts with Rows: 344 and Columns: 8. Each row after that shows one column, its type in angle brackets (such as <fct> for a factor or <dbl> for a decimal number), and the first few values.


Paste the output of penguins.info() and penguins.head(), not the data. penguins.info() gives the row count, column names, types and non-null counts. penguins.head() shows the first five rows, and those are real data values, so check them before you paste. For real research data, paste only penguins.info() (or penguins.dtypes) (see Card 7 in episode 02). Run this in Python:
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins
penguins = load_penguins()
penguins.info()
print(penguins.head())
penguins.info() reports 344 entries and 8 columns. Types show as str for text columns (pandas 2 prints object) and float64 for decimal numbers.



Do not paste the whole data set. The AI does not need every row, and the rest of the data may be sensitive in a real project. See episode 01 for what must stay out of a web AI tool.

title: 03. Anatomy of a Good Prompt
text:
Prompt 1: the quick version
make a graph of my data
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.

What typically goes wrong

The AI picks variables for you, and they may not be the ones you wanted.
It may use base R plotting, so the code does not match your tidyverse style. In Python it may mix plain matplotlib, pandas .plot() and seaborn.
It may invent column names, such as bill_len, because it cannot see your data.
It may give you several code blocks split by long explanations, so you cannot copy and run the code in one go.
It does not tell you how to check the plot.

title: 03. Anatomy of a Good Prompt
text:
Prompt 2: a better version

RPython


Before you use this prompt, run R.version.string and packageVersion("tidyverse") in the Console. Replace the bracketed text with the results and the glimpse() output from your own session.
I am using R, and my R version is [paste the output of R.version.string]. I am working in RStudio. I have tidyverse version [paste the output of packageVersion("tidyverse")] and palmerpenguins installed. I am not using any other packages.

My data is palmerpenguins::penguins. Here is the output of glimpse(penguins):
[paste the glimpse() output here]

Task: make a scatter plot of bill length (bill_length_mm, on the x axis) against flipper length (flipper_length_mm, on the y axis), with one point per penguin, coloured by species. Drop rows that are missing either measurement, and tell me how many rows you dropped.

Constraints:
- Use ggplot2 from the tidyverse, and use the native pipe |> to build the code.
- Do not use base R plotting or any package other than tidyverse and palmerpenguins.
- Use a colour-blind-safe colour scale, and name the function you used.
- Give the plot a title, axis labels with units (mm), and a legend title.

Output: one complete, runnable code block that works in a fresh R session after library(tidyverse) and library(palmerpenguins). Put a comment above each step. Save the plot to figures/ with ggsave(width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300).

Before the code, list your assumptions. After the code, tell me how to check that the plot is correct.


Before you use this prompt, run python --version in a terminal, and import pandas, seaborn; print(pandas.__version__, seaborn.__version__) in Python. Replace the bracketed text with the results and your own penguins.info() and penguins.head() output.

My data is loaded with: from palmerpenguins import load_penguins; penguins = load_penguins()
Here is the output of penguins.info():
[paste the penguins.info() output here]
And penguins.head():
[paste the penguins.head() output here]

Task: make a scatter plot of bill length (bill_length_mm, on the x axis) against flipper length (flipper_length_mm, on the y axis), with one point per penguin, coloured by species. Drop rows that are missing either measurement, and tell me how many rows you dropped.

Constraints:
- Use pandas for the data step and seaborn for the plot (matplotlib only for saving and labels).
- Do not use any package other than pandas, seaborn, matplotlib and palmerpenguins.
- Use a colour-blind-safe palette, and name it.

Output: one complete, runnable code block that works in a fresh Python session. Put a comment above each step. Save the plot to figures/ with dpi=300 at 7 by 5 inches.

Before the code, list your assumptions. After the code, tell me how to check that the plot is correct.










Part of the prompt
What it fixes




R (or Python) version and package versions
Stops the AI from using functions that your version does not have


glimpse() (or penguins.info() and penguins.head()) output

Removes the AI’s choice of what to plot

Keeps the code in tidyverse style, not a mix of base R and tidyverse


Colour-blind-safe scale and labels
Produces a plot you can read and publish

Shows you what the AI assumed, and gives you a way to test the result

    y = "Flipper length (mm)",

p

title: 03. Anatomy of a Good Prompt
text:
Iterate
A first answer rarely fits exactly. Ask a follow-up that names the change:
The points overlap heavily in the middle. Add a small amount of jitter, or use transparency, so that each point is visible. Keep everything else the same and give me the complete code block again.
Asking for “the complete code block again” stops the AI from giving you a fragment that you must merge by hand.
Three more follow-ups that help you learn, not just get code (adapted from Learning to Code with AI Chatbots):

Explain this code line by line for someone new to R. (or Python)
Mention anything you are uncertain about.
When stuck, do not just say “fix it”. Say: Here is what I expected and here is what happened. What am I missing?

title: 05. Wrangle with dplyr
text:
Time: 25 min · Track A (web AI) and Track B (agents)
Questions - How do dplyr verbs relate to the base R subsetting I already know? - How do I make an AI state exactly what it does with missing values? - How do I ask an AI for help with an error so that it can actually help?
Objectives - Read filter(), mutate(), group_by() and summarise() as base R operations. - Create penguins_clean and species_summary with a prompt that names the verbs, the NA policy and the pipe. - Write a debugging prompt that includes the code, the full error, your package versions and the result you expected.

title: 05. Wrangle with dplyr
text:
From Base R to dplyr
You already know how to subset a data frame with [rows, columns]. dplyr gives each common job its own verb, and the pipe |> passes the result of one step into the next. Read |> as “and then”.








Job
Base R
dplyr




Keep rows
penguins[!is.na(penguins$sex), ]
penguins |> filter(!is.na(sex))


Keep columns
penguins[, c("species", "sex")]
penguins |> select(species, sex)


Add a column
penguins$body_mass_kg <- penguins$body_mass_g / 1000
penguins |> mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000)


Summarise by group
tapply(penguins$body_mass_g, penguins$species, mean)
penguins |> group_by(species) |> summarise(mean = mean(body_mass_g))



Here is the cleaning step for this workshop, written both ways:
# Base R
penguins_clean_base <- penguins[!is.na(penguins$sex), ]
penguins_clean_base$body_mass_kg <- penguins_clean_base$body_mass_g / 1000

# dplyr
penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000)
Inside dplyr verbs you write sex, not penguins$sex: the verb looks up column names in the data frame you piped in.

title: 05. Wrangle with dplyr
text:
Clean and Summarise

Prompt 1: the quick version
clean the penguins data and summarise it
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

An NA policy you did not choose. AI code often uses drop_na() or na.omit(), which remove a row if any column is missing. On penguins this happens to give the same 333 rows as dropping missing sex, because the 2 rows with no measurements also lack sex. On your own data the two rules can give very different answers, and the AI rarely tells you which rows it removed.
na.rm left out, or added silently. mean(body_mass_g) on the raw data returns NA for Adelie and Gentoo. Some answers fix this by adding na.rm = TRUE everywhere, which hides how many values each mean used.
filter(sex != NA): this returns 0 rows, because any comparison with NA gives NA. Use !is.na(sex).
Superseded functions. %>% instead of |>, gather()/spread() instead of pivot_longer()/pivot_wider(), summarise_at() or mutate_each(). They still work (mostly), but they mix styles and confuse later prompts.
The grouping message. When you group by two columns, summarise() prints a message about regrouped output. The exact wording depends on your dplyr version. It is a message, not an error. Add .groups = "drop" to get an ungrouped result and no message.



Prompt 2: a better version
I am using R 4.x with the tidyverse and palmerpenguins. The data frame is
`penguins` with these columns:
<paste your glimpse(penguins) output here>

Write tidyverse code with the native pipe |> that:
1. creates penguins_clean: remove only the rows where sex is NA, then add a
   column body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000
2. creates species_summary: for each species, the number of penguins (n) and
   the mean and standard deviation of bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm and
   body_mass_g. Use .groups = "drop".

Use filter(), mutate(), group_by() and summarise(). Do not use drop_na(),
na.omit() or na.rm = TRUE: penguins_clean should have no missing values left.
After the code, give me base R lines (nrow, table, tapply) that I can use to
check the results.







Part of the prompt
What it fixes




remove only the rows where sex is NA
You choose the NA policy, not the AI


Object names penguins_clean, species_summary
Later episodes and the report depend on these names


Named verbs and |>
One consistent, current tidyverse style


Do not use drop_na(), na.omit() or na.rm = TRUE
No hidden row loss; a leftover NA shows up as NA


.groups = "drop"
No grouping surprises in the next step


give me base R lines … to check
Builds the cross-check into the answer

  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_bill_length = mean(bill_length_mm),
    sd_bill_length = sd(bill_length_mm),
    mean_flipper_length = mean(flipper_length_mm),
    sd_flipper_length = sd(flipper_length_mm),
    mean_body_mass = mean(body_mass_g),
    sd_body_mass = sd(body_mass_g),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

title: 05. Wrangle with dplyr
text:
Debug with an AI
Sooner or later, AI code (or your edit of it) fails. Say you want only the male penguins and run:
males <- penguins_clean |>
  filter(sex = "male")
R stops with:
Error in filter(penguins_clean, sex = "male") : We detected a named input.
ℹ This usually means that you've used `=` instead of `==`.
ℹ Did you mean `sex == "male"`?

Prompt 1: the quick version
my R code doesn't work
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

The AI has to guess. With no code and no error, it lists ten common R problems or asks you for details. You lose a round trip.
Half the error. Learners often paste only the last line. The first line says which function failed, and the ℹ lines often contain the fix.
A fix for the wrong version. Without package versions, the AI may suggest arguments that do not exist in your version, or an old workaround.
No expected result, so the AI cannot tell whether code that runs is actually right.
A rewrite instead of a fix. Asked vaguely, an AI may rewrite the whole script in a different style and introduce new problems.



Prompt 2: a better version
I am using R 4.x with dplyr (from the tidyverse) and palmerpenguins.
This code:

males <- penguins_clean |>
  filter(sex = "male")

gives this error:

Error in filter(penguins_clean, sex = "male") : We detected a named input.
ℹ This usually means that you've used `=` instead of `==`.
ℹ Did you mean `sex == "male"`?

Relevant lines from sessionInfo():
R version 4.x.x ...
other attached packages: dplyr_1.x.x ...

penguins_clean has 333 rows and a factor column sex with levels female and
male. I expected a data frame of the male penguins only.
Explain the cause in one or two sentences and give me the corrected line.
Do not change anything else.







Part of the prompt
What it fixes




The exact code that failed
The AI sees your mistake, not a guess at it


The full error, copied from the Console
Includes the function name and R’s own hint


sessionInfo() lines
Fixes match your R and package versions


What the data look like and what you expected
The AI can judge whether a fix is correct


corrected line … do not change anything else
A small fix you can read, not a rewrite






Example AI output (instructor testing)

Tool: [AI tool, e.g. Google Search AI Mode] · Date tested: [YYYY-MM-DD]
Code returned:
males <- penguins_clean |>
  filter(sex == "male")

nrow(males)
Output when run:
[1] 168
Notes: The fix changed only = to ==, as asked. 168 male penguins, matching table(penguins_clean$sex).

Run sessionInfo() in the Console and copy the R version and the “other attached packages” lines. Paste no data.


Check it
Run the corrected code and check it with base R:

  filter(sex == "male")

nrow(males)                       # 168
table(penguins_clean$sex)         # female 165, male 168
Other errors worth knowing on sight:

Column `bill_length_mm` doesn't exist: you have the base R penguins (episode 04). Run library(palmerpenguins).

  filter(sex == "male")

nrow(males)  # 168







Tip



Agent extension (Track B) Give the agent the wrangling task with acceptance criteria:

(remove only rows where sex is NA; add body_mass_kg) and species_summary
(n, mean and sd of bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g by species,
.groups = "drop"). Use |> and no na.rm. Run the script with Rscript.

species_summary$body_mass_mean equals tapply(...) to 3 decimal places.

title: 07. Statistics: Code You Can Run but Do Not Understand
text:
Time: 15 min · Track A (web AI) and Track B (agents)
Questions - Why is a confident AI answer to a statistics question dangerous? - How do I use an AI to understand model output, not just produce it?
Objectives - Show Simpson’s paradox in the penguins data with lm(). - Fit mass_model and check one AI claim about summary(mass_model) yourself. - Optional: ask an AI when a t-test would be wrong, and act on the answer.

title: 07. Statistics: Code You Can Run but Do Not Understand
text:
Bill Length and Bill Depth

Prompt 1: the quick version
Is there a relationship between bill length and bill depth in penguins? Give me R code.
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

One regression for all penguins. The usual answer is lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = penguins) or cor.test(), with a conclusion like “longer bills are slightly shallower (negative correlation)”.
The conclusion is backwards for every species. The penguins data contain three species, and species is a confounder: Gentoo penguins have long but shallow bills. Pooling them reverses the relationship. This is Simpson’s paradox.
Confident wording. A small p-value is presented as a finding, with no mention of grouping, confounders or assumptions.



Prompt 2: a better version
I am using R with the tidyverse and the data frame penguins_clean
(palmerpenguins columns). The data contain three species.

I want to know how bill_depth_mm relates to bill_length_mm.
1. Fit the relationship for all penguins together, then separately within
   each species, using lm() and the native pipe |>.
2. Tell me whether the two answers could disagree, and why.
3. List the variables in this dataset that could confound the relationship.
Do not state a conclusion until I have run the code.







Part of the prompt
What it fixes




The data contain three species
Puts the grouping in front of the AI


all together, then within each species
Asks for both fits, so you can compare them


could … disagree, and why
Invites the Simpson’s paradox explanation instead of one answer


List … confounders
Makes the AI reason about the design, not just the code


Do not state a conclusion until I have run the code
You see the numbers before any interpretation






Example AI output (instructor testing)

Tool: [AI tool, e.g. Google Search AI Mode] · Date tested: [YYYY-MM-DD]
Code returned:
# 1a. All penguins together
fit_all <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = penguins_clean)
coef(fit_all)

# 1b. Separately within each species
penguins_clean |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    intercept = coef(lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm))[1],
    slope = coef(lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm))[2]
  )
Output when run:
   (Intercept) bill_length_mm
   20.78664867    -0.08232675
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  species   intercept slope
  <fct>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 Adelie        11.5  0.177
2 Chinstrap      7.57 0.222
3 Gentoo         5.12 0.208
Notes: Overall slope −0.082; within-species slopes 0.177, 0.222 and 0.208, matching the Check it values. Read the AI’s explanation of why they disagree before accepting it.



Check it
Run both fits and compare the slopes:
coef(lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = penguins_clean))

penguins_clean |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(slope = coef(lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm))[2])
The second block is deliberately denser than anything so far: inside summarise(), lm() fits one model per species, coef() returns its intercept and slope, and [2] keeps the slope. Read it from the inside out. If an AI gives you code like this, ask it to explain each layer before you run it.
Across all 333 penguins, the slope is −0.082 mm of depth per mm of length. Within species, the slopes are 0.177 (Adelie), 0.222 (Chinstrap) and 0.208 (Gentoo). All three are positive. Look back at p_bill from episode 06: each species’ line slopes up, while the three clusters as a whole run downhill.


Reference solution

# All penguins together: slope -0.082
coef(lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = penguins_clean))

# Within each species: 0.177, 0.222, 0.208
penguins_clean |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(slope = coef(lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm))[2])

title: 07. Statistics: Code You Can Run but Do Not Understand
text:
Body Mass by Species
Fit the model the report uses:
mass_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_clean)
summary(mass_model)
anova(mass_model)

Prompt 1: the quick version
what does this mean?
<pasted summary(mass_model) output>
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

“Chinstrap penguins are not different.” A p-value of 0.691 means the data do not show a difference from Adelie. That is not evidence that there is none.
Wrong reference level. The AI may describe speciesGentoo as the mean Gentoo mass. It is the difference from the reference level, Adelie.
Assumptions skipped. lm() assumes independent penguins, roughly normal residuals and similar spread in each group. A general answer rarely checks these.
Over-reach. “Species causes body mass differences” from observational data.



Prompt 2: a better version
I fitted lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_clean) in R, where species
is a factor with levels Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo. Here is summary() output:

<paste summary(mass_model) output>

Explain each part of the output (Call, Residuals, each Coefficients row and
column, Residual standard error, R-squared, F-statistic) in plain language for
a biologist. Say which species is the reference level and what the intercept
means. List the assumptions of this model and what would make the conclusions
wrong. Finish with one claim from your explanation that I can check myself in
base R, and the code to check it.







Part of the prompt
What it fixes




The model formula and factor levels
The AI knows how R coded the comparison


Explain each part
A line-by-line explanation, not a one-line verdict


which species is the reference level
Prevents misreading the coefficients


assumptions … what would make the conclusions wrong
Surfaces the caveats your Limitations section needs


one claim … I can check myself
Turns the explanation into something you verify






Example AI output (instructor testing)

Tool: [AI tool, e.g. Google Search AI Mode] · Date tested: [YYYY-MM-DD]
Code returned:
# Claim to check: the intercept is the mean body mass of Adelie penguins,
# and each other coefficient is that species' mean minus the Adelie mean.
means <- tapply(penguins_clean$body_mass_g, penguins_clean$species, mean)
means
means - means["Adelie"]
Output when run:
   Adelie Chinstrap    Gentoo
 3706.164  3733.088  5092.437
    Adelie  Chinstrap     Gentoo
   0.00000   26.92385 1386.27259
Notes: The Chinstrap and Gentoo differences (26.92, 1386.27) match the coefficients in summary(mass_model), so the AI’s claim about the reference level holds.



Check it
Check one claim yourself. The intercept should be the mean Adelie body mass, and each other coefficient should be a difference from Adelie:
tapply(penguins_clean$body_mass_g, penguins_clean$species, mean)
You should get Adelie 3706.164, Chinstrap 3733.088 and Gentoo 5092.437. The intercept in summary(mass_model) is 3706.16. The Gentoo coefficient is 1386.27, which is 5092.437 − 3706.164. The Chinstrap coefficient (26.92) is 3733.088 − 3706.164. Species explains about 67% of the variation in body mass (R² = 0.6745).
If the AI’s explanation got any of this wrong, note what it was. That is the kind of error you would otherwise have put in your report.


Optional: a t-test, and when it would be wrong






Note



If you have time. This section is optional. If you are short of time, skip to the Key points; the report in episode 08 does not need the t-test.


Ask your AI assistant: “Write R code for a t-test of whether male and female penguins differ in body mass, and tell me when this test would be wrong.”
A typical answer is t.test(body_mass_g ~ sex, data = penguins_clean), which runs and gives a tiny p-value. Before you trust it, ask:

Are the groups comparable? This test pools three species of very different size, so the “male” and “female” groups are each a mixture. Compare within one species instead.
Which t-test? R’s t.test() runs Welch’s test (unequal variances) by default. Many AI explanations describe Student’s test with equal variances.
Are the observations independent? One row per penguin, measured once. Check this for your own data.

adelie <- penguins_clean |>
  filter(species == "Adelie")
t.test(body_mass_g ~ sex, data = adelie)
Within Adelie penguins, males are on average 675 g heavier (females 3368.8 g, males 4043.5 g; 95% CI for the female minus male difference: −776 to −573 g).


Reference solution

mass_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_clean)
summary(mass_model)
anova(mass_model)

# Check: intercept = Adelie mean; Gentoo coefficient = Gentoo mean - Adelie mean
tapply(penguins_clean$body_mass_g, penguins_clean$species, mean)

# t-test within one species, not pooled across species
adelie <- penguins_clean |>
  filter(species == "Adelie")
t.test(body_mass_g ~ sex, data = adelie)
Catch-up file: checkpoints/after-07.R.



Optional: a review-only second opinion
Paste your code into a fresh chat (or a different AI assistant) and ask:
Review this code only. Do not change it. List any errors, and the
assumptions this analysis makes.
A fresh chat has not seen the earlier explanation, so it is less likely to repeat it. Check each point it raises yourself; it can be wrong too (Carpentries: coding with LLMs).






Tip



Agent extension (Track B)
Add a "07 Statistics" section to analysis.R: the overall and per-species
slopes of bill_depth_mm on bill_length_mm, mass_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~
species, data = penguins_clean) with summary() and anova(), and a within-Adelie
t-test of body_mass_g by sex. Run the script. Acceptance: the overall slope is
negative and all three species slopes are positive; the model intercept equals
the Adelie mean from tapply(). Then write three sentences I could put in a
Limitations section, and list any claim you are not sure of.
Agents explain output as confidently as web AIs. Verify one claim from its explanation yourself before you accept the edit.

title: 07. Statistics: Code You Can Run but Do Not Understand
text:
Key points

Pooling groups can reverse a relationship (Simpson’s paradox). Ask the AI about grouping and confounders, then fit both ways.
An overall summary can hide or reverse what happens in subgroups, so report results by group when groups differ; fairness audits use the same check (Carpentries: FAIR explainable ML).
Ask the AI to explain each part of summary() output, then check one claim with base R.
Ask what would make a test wrong before you report it.
If you cannot explain a result, it does not go in the report. Record what you did not check in the Limitations section.

Questions - How do pandas method chains relate to the indexing I already know? - How do I make an AI state exactly what it does with missing values? - How do I ask an AI for help with an error so that it can actually help?

title: 05. Wrangle with pandas
text:
From Indexing to Method Chains
You already know how to subset a data frame with [] and .loc[]. pandas also gives each common job a method that returns a new data frame, so you can write the steps one after another as a method chain. Read each . at the start of a line as “and then”. The outer brackets let the chain run over several lines.








Job
Indexing
Method chain




Keep rows
penguins[penguins["sex"].notna()]
penguins.dropna(subset=["sex"])


Keep columns
penguins[["species", "sex"]]
penguins.loc[:, ["species", "sex"]]


Add a column
penguins["body_mass_kg"] = penguins["body_mass_g"] / 1000
penguins.assign(body_mass_kg=lambda df: df["body_mass_g"] / 1000)


Summarise by group
a loop over species with .loc[mask, "body_mass_g"].mean()
penguins.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"].mean()



Here is the cleaning step for this workshop, written both ways:
# Indexing
penguins_clean_idx = penguins.loc[penguins["sex"].notna()].copy()
penguins_clean_idx["body_mass_kg"] = penguins_clean_idx["body_mass_g"] / 1000

# Method chain
penguins_clean = (
    penguins
    .dropna(subset=["sex"])
    .assign(body_mass_kg=lambda df: df["body_mass_g"] / 1000)
)
Inside assign(), lambda df: means “the data frame at this step of the chain”. The chain never changes penguins; it builds a new data frame. That also avoids the copy warnings you meet in the indexing version if you leave out .copy().

title: 05. Wrangle with pandas
text:
Clean and Summarise

Prompt 1: the quick version
clean the penguins data and summarise it with pandas
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

An NA policy you did not choose. AI code often uses dropna() with no arguments, which removes a row if any column is missing. On penguins this happens to give the same 333 rows as dropping missing sex, because the 2 rows with no measurements also lack sex. On your own data the two rules can give very different answers, and the AI rarely tells you which rows it removed.
Missing values skipped without a word. pandas mean() and std() skip NaN by default (skipna=True). On the raw data, the Adelie mean body mass is 3700.7 g from 151 penguins; after cleaning it is 3706.2 g from 146. Neither result mentions how many values it used. value_counts() also drops NaN unless you pass dropna=False.
Comparing with NaN. penguins[penguins["sex"] != np.nan] keeps all 344 rows, because NaN is never equal to anything, itself included. == None keeps none. Use .notna() or dropna(subset=...).
inplace=True. penguins_clean = penguins.dropna(subset=["sex"], inplace=True) changes penguins and sets penguins_clean to None. The next step fails with AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'assign'.
Chained assignment. penguins[penguins["sex"].notna()]["body_mass_kg"] = ... never changes penguins. pandas 2 warns with SettingWithCopyWarning; pandas 3 warns with ChainedAssignmentError and says the assignment “never works”. Adding a column to a filtered subset without .copy() gives the same SettingWithCopyWarning on pandas 2 and no warning on pandas 3.
Removed and mismatched functions. df.append() was removed in pandas 2.0 (AttributeError: 'DataFrame' object has no attribute 'append'); use pd.concat(). np.std() divides by n, while pandas std() divides by n − 1, so the two give different standard deviations.



Prompt 2: a better version
I am using Python 3.x with pandas 2.x and palmerpenguins. The data frame is
`penguins`, loaded with load_penguins(). penguins.info() gives:
<paste your penguins.info() output here>

Write pandas code as method chains (one method per line, inside brackets) that:
1. creates penguins_clean: remove only the rows where sex is missing, with
   dropna(subset=["sex"]), then add a column body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000
   with assign()
2. creates species_summary: for each species, the number of penguins (n) and
   the mean and standard deviation of bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm and
   body_mass_g. Use groupby("species", as_index=False) and agg() with named
   aggregations.

Do not use inplace=True, chained assignment or .append(). penguins_clean
should have no missing values left. After the code, give me plain pandas lines
(len, value_counts, .loc with a boolean mask) that I can use to check the
results.

What it fixes

You choose the NA policy, not the AI

One consistent, current pandas style

No None objects, copy warnings or removed methods


no missing values left
Every later mean uses all the rows you kept

Builds the cross-check into the answer

title: 07. Statistics: Code You Can Run but Do Not Understand
text:
Time: 15 min · Track A (web AI) and Track B (agents)
Questions - Why is a confident AI answer to a statistics question dangerous? - How do I use an AI to understand model output, not just produce it?
Objectives - Show Simpson’s paradox in the penguins data with smf.ols(). - Fit mass_model and check one AI claim about mass_model.summary() yourself. - Optional: ask an AI when a t-test would be wrong, and act on the answer.
An AI assistant makes it trivial to produce statistical output. It does not make you able to interpret it. The rule for this episode, and for your report: if you cannot explain it, it does not go in the report.
This episode uses the statsmodels formula interface, which reads model formulas the same way R does:

title: 07. Statistics: Code You Can Run but Do Not Understand
text:
Bill Length and Bill Depth

Prompt 1: the quick version
Is there a relationship between bill length and bill depth in penguins? Give me Python code.
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

One regression for all penguins. The usual answer is smf.ols("bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm", data=penguins).fit(), scipy.stats.linregress() or a correlation, with a conclusion like “longer bills are slightly shallower (negative correlation)”.
The conclusion is backwards for every species. The penguins data contain three species, and species is a confounder: Gentoo penguins have long but shallow bills. Pooling them reverses the relationship. This is Simpson’s paradox.
A model with no intercept. sm.OLS(y, X) without sm.add_constant(X) forces the line through zero. On penguins it gives a slope of +0.383, a different answer again, with no warning. The formula interface (smf.ols()) adds the intercept for you.
Correlation on the whole data frame. penguins.corr() stops with ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'Adelie' on pandas 2 and later. The “fix”, corr(numeric_only=True), returns −0.235 for bill length and depth, which hides the paradox too.
Confident wording. A small p-value is presented as a finding, with no mention of grouping, confounders or assumptions.



Prompt 2: a better version
I am using Python with pandas and statsmodels, and the data frame
penguins_clean (palmerpenguins columns). The data contain three species.

I want to know how bill_depth_mm relates to bill_length_mm.
1. Fit the relationship for all penguins together, then separately within
   each species, using statsmodels.formula.api.ols.
2. Tell me whether the two answers could disagree, and why.
3. List the variables in this dataset that could confound the relationship.
Do not state a conclusion until I have run the code.







Part of the prompt
What it fixes




The data contain three species
Puts the grouping in front of the AI


all together, then within each species
Asks for both fits, so you can compare them


statsmodels.formula.api.ols
A formula with an intercept, not a bare sm.OLS()


could … disagree, and why
Invites the Simpson’s paradox explanation instead of one answer


List … confounders
Makes the AI reason about the design, not just the code


Do not state a conclusion until I have run the code
You see the numbers before any interpretation






Example AI output (instructor testing)

Tool: [AI tool, e.g. Google Search AI Mode] · Date tested: [YYYY-MM-DD]
Code returned:
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

# 1. All penguins together
overall = smf.ols("bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm", data=penguins_clean).fit()
print("All penguins:", round(overall.params["bill_length_mm"], 3))

# 2. Within each species
for sp, df in penguins_clean.groupby("species"):
    fit = smf.ols("bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm", data=df).fit()
    print(sp, round(fit.params["bill_length_mm"], 3))
Output when run:
All penguins: -0.082
Adelie 0.177
Chinstrap 0.222
Gentoo 0.208
Notes: [What worked, what needed fixing, anything worth showing learners]



Check it
Run both fits, then check the slopes with a second method, np.polyfit(), which fits a straight line without statsmodels:
overall_fit = smf.ols("bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm", data=penguins_clean).fit()
print(overall_fit.params["bill_length_mm"])

for species, group in penguins_clean.groupby("species"):
    print(species, np.polyfit(group["bill_length_mm"], group["bill_depth_mm"], 1)[0])
Across all 333 penguins, the slope is −0.082 mm of depth per mm of length. Within species, the slopes are 0.177 (Adelie), 0.222 (Chinstrap) and 0.208 (Gentoo). All three are positive. Look back at p_bill from episode 06: each species’ line slopes up, while the three clusters as a whole run downhill.


Reference solution

# All penguins together: slope -0.082
overall_fit = smf.ols("bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm", data=penguins_clean).fit()
print(overall_fit.params)

# Within each species: 0.177, 0.222, 0.208
slopes = {}
for species, group in penguins_clean.groupby("species"):
    fit = smf.ols("bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm", data=group).fit()
    slopes[species] = fit.params["bill_length_mm"]
species_slopes = pd.Series(slopes, name="slope")
print(species_slopes)

title: 07. Statistics: Code You Can Run but Do Not Understand
text:
Body Mass by Species
Fit the model the report uses:
mass_model = smf.ols("body_mass_g ~ species", data=penguins_clean).fit()
print(mass_model.summary())
print(sm.stats.anova_lm(mass_model))

Prompt 1: the quick version
what does this mean?
<pasted mass_model.summary() output>
Try it in your AI assistant before reading on.


What typically goes wrong

“Chinstrap penguins are not different.” A p-value of 0.691 means the data do not show a difference from Adelie. That is not evidence that there is none.
Wrong reference level. The AI may describe species[T.Gentoo] as the mean Gentoo mass. It is the difference from the reference level, Adelie. statsmodels picks the first level in alphabetical order; T. stands for treatment coding.
Over-reading the bottom block. statsmodels prints Omnibus, Durbin-Watson, Jarque-Bera and Cond. No. under every model. Durbin-Watson (2.989 here) tests for correlation between neighbouring rows, which only means something when row order means something, such as a time series. An AI often interprets every number it is shown.
Assumptions skipped. OLS assumes independent penguins, roughly normal residuals and similar spread in each group. A general answer rarely checks these.
Over-reach. “Species causes body mass differences” from observational data.



Prompt 2: a better version
I fitted smf.ols("body_mass_g ~ species", data=penguins_clean).fit() with
statsmodels in Python, where species is a text column with the values Adelie,
Chinstrap and Gentoo. Here is the summary() output:

<paste print(mass_model.summary()) output>

Explain each part of the output (the top block including R-squared and
F-statistic, each coefficient row and column, and the bottom block with
Omnibus, Durbin-Watson, Jarque-Bera and Cond. No.) in plain language for a
biologist. Say which species is the reference level and what the Intercept
means, and which numbers in the bottom block do not apply to these data.
List the assumptions of this model and what would make the conclusions wrong.
Finish with one claim from your explanation that I can check myself with
plain pandas, and the code to check it.







Part of the prompt
What it fixes




The model formula and the species values
The AI knows how statsmodels coded the comparison


Explain each part
A line-by-line explanation, not a one-line verdict


which species is the reference level
Prevents misreading the coefficients


which numbers … do not apply
Stops the AI interpreting Durbin-Watson for unordered data


assumptions … what would make the conclusions wrong
Surfaces the caveats your Limitations section needs


one claim … I can check myself
Turns the explanation into something you verify






Example AI output (instructor testing)

Tool: [AI tool, e.g. Google Search AI Mode] · Date tested: [YYYY-MM-DD]
Code returned:
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

mass_model = smf.ols("body_mass_g ~ species", data=penguins_clean).fit()

# Claim: the Intercept is the mean Adelie mass, and each coefficient
# is that species' mean minus the Adelie mean.
means = penguins_clean.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"].mean()
print(mass_model.params.round(1))
print(means.round(1))
print(round(means["Gentoo"] - means["Adelie"], 1))
Output when run:
Intercept               3706.2
species[T.Chinstrap]      26.9
species[T.Gentoo]       1386.3
dtype: float64
species
Adelie       3706.2
Chinstrap    3733.1
Gentoo       5092.4
Name: body_mass_g, dtype: float64
1386.3
Notes: [What worked, what needed fixing, anything worth showing learners]



Check it
Check one claim yourself. The intercept should be the mean Adelie body mass, and each other coefficient should be a difference from Adelie:
for species in ["Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"]:
    mask = penguins_clean["species"] == species
    print(species, penguins_clean.loc[mask, "body_mass_g"].mean())

print(mass_model.params)
print(mass_model.rsquared)
You should get Adelie 3706.164, Chinstrap 3733.088 and Gentoo 5092.437. The Intercept in mass_model.summary() is 3706.16. The species[T.Gentoo] coefficient is 1386.27, which is 5092.437 − 3706.164. The species[T.Chinstrap] coefficient (26.92) is 3733.088 − 3706.164. Species explains about 67% of the variation in body mass: the summary rounds R² to 0.674, and mass_model.rsquared gives 0.6745.
If the AI’s explanation got any of this wrong, note what it was. That is the kind of error you would otherwise have put in your report.


Optional: a t-test, and when it would be wrong






Note



If you have time. This section is optional. If you are short of time, skip to the Key points; the report in episode 08 does not need the t-test.


Ask your AI assistant: “Write Python code for a t-test of whether male and female penguins differ in body mass, and tell me when this test would be wrong.”
A typical answer is stats.ttest_ind(male, female) from scipy, run on all penguins, which gives a tiny p-value. Before you trust it, ask:

Are the groups comparable? This test pools three species of very different size, so the “male” and “female” groups are each a mixture. Compare within one species instead.
Which t-test? scipy’s ttest_ind() runs Student’s test (equal variances) by default. R’s t.test() runs Welch’s test. Pass equal_var=False for Welch’s test, and check which one the AI’s explanation describes.
Are the observations independent? One row per penguin, measured once. Check this for your own data.

adelie = penguins_clean[penguins_clean["species"] == "Adelie"]
female_mass = adelie.loc[adelie["sex"] == "female", "body_mass_g"]
male_mass = adelie.loc[adelie["sex"] == "male", "body_mass_g"]

t_result = stats.ttest_ind(female_mass, male_mass, equal_var=False)
print(t_result)
print(t_result.confidence_interval())  # needs scipy 1.11 or later
print(female_mass.mean(), male_mass.mean())
Within Adelie penguins, males are on average 675 g heavier (females 3368.8 g, males 4043.5 g; 95% CI for the female minus male difference: −776 to −573 g).


Reference solution

mass_model = smf.ols("body_mass_g ~ species", data=penguins_clean).fit()
print(mass_model.summary())
print(sm.stats.anova_lm(mass_model))

# Check: Intercept = Adelie mean; Gentoo coefficient = Gentoo mean - Adelie mean
for species in ["Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"]:
    print(species, penguins_clean.loc[penguins_clean["species"] == species, "body_mass_g"].mean())

# t-test within one species, not pooled across species; Welch's test
adelie = penguins_clean[penguins_clean["species"] == "Adelie"]
female_mass = adelie.loc[adelie["sex"] == "female", "body_mass_g"]
male_mass = adelie.loc[adelie["sex"] == "male", "body_mass_g"]
t_result = stats.ttest_ind(female_mass, male_mass, equal_var=False)
print(t_result)
print(t_result.confidence_interval())
Catch-up file: checkpoints/after-07.py.



Optional: a review-only second opinion
Paste your code into a fresh chat (or a different AI assistant) and ask:
Review this code only. Do not change it. List any errors, and the
assumptions this analysis makes.
A fresh chat has not seen the earlier explanation, so it is less likely to repeat it. Check each point it raises yourself; it can be wrong too (Carpentries: coding with LLMs).






Tip



Agent extension (Track B)
Add a "07 Statistics" section to analysis.py: the overall and per-species
slopes of bill_depth_mm on bill_length_mm with smf.ols(),
mass_model = smf.ols("body_mass_g ~ species", data=penguins_clean).fit()
with summary() and sm.stats.anova_lm(), and a within-Adelie Welch t-test
(equal_var=False) of body_mass_g by sex. Run the script. Acceptance: the
overall slope is negative and all three species slopes are positive; the
Intercept equals the Adelie mean from a .loc boolean mask. Then write three
sentences I could put in a Limitations section, and list any claim you are
not sure of.
Agents explain output as confidently as web AIs. Verify one claim from its explanation yourself before you accept the edit.

title: 07. Statistics: Code You Can Run but Do Not Understand
text:
Key points

Pooling groups can reverse a relationship (Simpson’s paradox). Ask the AI about grouping and confounders, then fit both ways.
An overall summary can hide or reverse what happens in subgroups, so report results by group when groups differ; fairness audits use the same check (Carpentries: FAIR explainable ML).
Use the formula interface, smf.ols(), so the model has an intercept.
Ask the AI to explain each part of summary() output, including which parts do not apply, then check one claim with plain pandas.
Ask what would make a test wrong before you report it. scipy’s ttest_ind() assumes equal variances unless you pass equal_var=False.
If you cannot explain a result, it does not go in the report. Record what you did not check in the Limitations section.

These are the mistakes an AI assistant makes most often in this workshop. Use them as teaching moments. Learners remember a failure they found themselves far longer than a warning you gave them.
AI output varies from run to run and between tools. Treat each entry as a pattern to look for, not a response you can predict. Before you teach a failure, reproduce it yourself on the day, and note the wording and tool that produced it.

title: AI Failure Modes
text:
Two Penguins Datasets
What happens. R 4.5 and later ship datasets::penguins, with short column names such as bill_len, bill_dep, flipper_len and body_mass. The palmerpenguins package uses bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm and body_mass_g. An AI assistant may write code for either version, without saying which one it chose.
Teaching moment. Ask learners to run the code the AI gives them. If it fails with “object not found” or “column doesn’t exist”, ask them which dataset the code uses. This failure makes a useful Check it exercise: the learner sees the mismatch, names the cause, and asks the AI to fix its own code with the dataset named in the prompt.

title: AI Failure Modes
text:
Pipe Style
What happens. The native pipe |> arrived in R 4.1. Many AI answers still use the magrittr pipe %>%, which library(tidyverse) also makes available. Both pipes run in a tidyverse session, but mixed styles make a report harder to read.
Teaching moment. Put |> in the prompt. Then ask learners to find any %>% in the output and decide whether to change it. The workshop style is native pipe throughout.

title: AI Failure Modes
text:
Superseded Arguments
What happens. ggplot2 3.4.0 replaced size = with linewidth = for lines. The old argument still runs with a deprecation warning, so learners may not notice. Likewise, tidyr::gather() and tidyr::spread() are superseded by pivot_longer() and pivot_wider(). Code with the old names still runs, but it signals an out-of-date source.
Teaching moment. Point out the deprecation warning when it appears. Ask learners to read the warning and check the function’s help page for the current argument name. Put the style rule in the prompt so the AI does not use the old name.

title: AI Failure Modes
text:
Invented Functions and Arguments
What happens. An AI assistant may call a function that does not exist, or pass an argument that a real function does not accept. Its explanation of the invented call often sounds sure of itself. Learners who cannot read R code well may not notice until the code fails.
Teaching moment. Ask learners to run ?function_name for any function they do not recognise. If the help page does not list the argument, the AI made it up. Ask the AI to cite the help page, then check the citation yourself.

title: AI Failure Modes
text:
Silently Dropped NA Values
What happens. Some functions drop missing values without a warning, and others return NA as the result. Filtering with filter() removes rows where the condition is NA. A summary that quietly excludes rows can change the numbers in the report. The penguins_clean object in episode 05 removes the 11 incomplete rows on purpose, so an unexplained change in row count is a warning sign.
Teaching moment. Ask learners to count rows before and after each step with nrow(). Then ask the AI what it did with the missing values. A good answer names the rows it removed. A poor answer does not mention them.

title: AI Failure Modes
text:
Wrong Statistical Interpretation
What happens. An AI assistant often explains a p-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true, or treats a non-significant result as proof of no effect. Its interpretation can also ignore the assumptions of a test. The wording sounds confident, so learners tend to copy it into the report.
Teaching moment. Use episode 07. Ask the AI to explain each line of the summary() output, then compare its explanation with a reference you trust. Ask it to name the assumptions and the conditions that would make the result wrong. Learners check one claim themselves before they accept any of them.

title: AI Failure Modes
text:
Simpson’s Paradox
What happens. In the penguins data, bill depth and bill length have a negative slope across all species combined, but a positive slope within each species. An AI answer that uses the pooled data gives a confident and wrong conclusion.
Teaching moment. Ask learners to plot the data twice, once pooled and once coloured by species. Then ask the AI what the two plots show. The better prompt in episode 07 asks about grouping and confounders. Use it to show why prompt wording changes the answer.

title: AI Failure Modes
text:
Invented Slurm Modules and Partitions
What happens. An AI assistant may invent a module name, such as an R or conda module with a version that the cluster does not install. It may also name a partition, account or resource limit that the cluster does not use. The script looks reasonable, and fails only when the scheduler rejects it.
Teaching moment. Ask learners to run module spider on the cluster, or to check the documentation, before they accept any module name. Show how the AI’s invented name differs from the real one. Do not criticise the learner who accepted it. Ask them to explain how they would check the name next time.

title: AI Failure Modes
section: Smart Quotes From Copy and Paste
text:
Smart Quotes From Copy and Paste
What happens. Web pages and word processors replace straight quotes (" and ') with curly quotes (“ ” and ‘ ’). R rejects curly quotes, and the error message does not explain why. The same code can look correct on screen.
Teaching moment. Ask learners to paste a line with a string into the R console, then read the error. Show them how to replace the curly quotes with straight quotes in the editor, using Find and Replace. Suggest that learners check the code in the editor before they run it.

title: AI Failure Modes
text:
Truncated Code in AI Mode
What happens. Google Search AI Mode answers are short and grounded in search results. For long code, it may cut the answer short or replace part of it with a comment such as # ... rest of code.
Teaching moment. Add “give the complete code in one block” to the prompt. If the code is still cut short, ask the AI to continue from the last line. Show learners that the prompt is the fix, not a fault in their own code.
Fallback. If AI Mode is unavailable or truncates too often, switch to Duck.ai or logged-out ChatGPT, as the Track A backups. Use the same prompts. Note the tool change in the session notes.

title: AI Failure Modes
text:
Confidently Wrong Explanations
What happens. An AI assistant may explain the output with fluent prose that contradicts the output. It can describe a plot that does not match the code, or claim a result the output does not show. Learners often trust the prose more than the numbers.
Teaching moment. Ask learners to find one claim in the explanation and check it against the output. The habit matters more than any single error. Use episode 10 to close the session with the human checklist.

title: AI Failure Modes
section: Outdated Quarto and R Markdown YAML
text:
Outdated Quarto and R Markdown YAML
What happens. Older R Markdown templates use output: html_document in the YAML header. A Quarto document uses a format: key, and its YAML options differ from R Markdown. An AI assistant may mix the two, which produces a report that fails to render or renders without the options learners expect.
Teaching moment. In episode 08, ask learners to check the YAML header against the Quarto documentation before they render. Point out that quarto render penguins_report.qmd reads the header, so one wrong key can change the whole report.

title: Demo Script
text:
This script covers the live-coding demo for episodes 03 to 08. Use Google Search AI Mode on a projected screen, signed out, as the Track A tool. The demo follows the same weak-then-better pattern as the learner episodes, so learners see the method before they try it.
AI output varies. Read each “What to point out” item as a likely outcome, and rehearse each prompt before the session to see what your tool returns on the day. Do not promise learners a particular answer.
The demo runs in R. Python learners in the room follow the same prompts from python/, which mirror each R episode. Mention once, at episode 04, that their Prompt 2 blocks name the Python version, pandas and seaborn and paste penguins.info() and penguins.head() instead of glimpse(), and that the Check it numbers are the same.

title: Demo Script
text:
Before You Start

Open a private window and sign out of Google. Load AI Mode, and check that it answers a simple question.
Open the RStudio project ml103-penguins in a second window, with analysis.R ready. Do not type into it until the demo reaches that step.
Keep the Prompt 1 and Prompt 2 blocks from each episode open in a text editor. Copy from the text file, not from the web page, so you avoid smart quotes in the prompt.
Have ai-failure-modes.md open for the entry that matches each episode.

title: Demo Script
section: How to Run Each Episode Segment
text:
How to Run Each Episode Segment
For each episode:

Type the weak prompt (Prompt 1) into AI Mode, and say why you chose it. Do not explain the problems yet.
Show the answer. Pause, and ask learners what they notice. Then point out the failures listed below, if they appear.
Type the better prompt (Prompt 2) into a new AI Mode session, and say which part of the prompt you changed.
Paste the code into the project file, run it, and do the Check it step aloud.

Think aloud while you read the AI’s answer: say what you expected, where you hesitate, and what you would check (adapted from GenAI in Workshops: Instructor Training Bonus Module).
If AI Mode returns truncated code, add “give the complete code in one block” and ask again.

title: Demo Script
section: Episode 03: Anatomy of a Good Prompt
text:
Episode 03: Anatomy of a Good Prompt
Weak prompt. “make a graph of my data”. Type it, and show the answer, which will probably ask for more information.
What to point out.

The answer often asks for the data, the variables and the package. Name each missing piece aloud. That is the lesson of this episode.
Then type the better prompt from episode 03, which names the data shape, the package, the style and the output.

Close. Ask learners to name the four or five parts of the better prompt before you move on.

title: Demo Script
text:
Episode 04: Load and Explore Penguins
Weak prompt. “analyse the penguins data in R”. Type it, and show the answer.
What to point out.

The answer may use the datasets::penguins short names (bill_len, flipper_len) instead of palmerpenguins. Run the code and show the error if it appears. This is the Two Penguins Datasets failure in ai-failure-modes.md.
The answer may use base R or tidyverse, or both, without saying which.

Better prompt. Type the Prompt 2 block, which names the R version, the tidyverse and palmerpenguins, and includes the glimpse() output. Paste the output from your own session, not from the text file, so learners see real output.
Close. Show that glimpse(penguins) in your session matches the column names in the better prompt.

title: Demo Script
text:
Episode 05: Wrangle with dplyr
Weak prompt. “clean the penguins data and summarise it”. Type it, and show the answer.
What to point out.

The answer may remove rows without saying how many, or may choose its own rule for missing values. Count the rows before and after with nrow(), as learners will do in the episode. See Silently Dropped NA Values.
The answer may use %>%. Point out the pipe style, then compare it with the better prompt, which asks for |>.

Better prompt. Type the Prompt 2 block, which names the verbs, the NA policy and the base R cross-check. Run the cross-check and show that the row counts match.
Close. Ask learners what they would have to check if the cross-check failed.

title: Demo Script
text:
Episode 06: Visualise with ggplot2
Weak prompt. “plot penguins in ggplot”. Type it, and show the answer.
What to point out.

The answer may pick the variables for you, or may use size = for a line. See Superseded Arguments.
Copying code from the answer into RStudio may produce an error about curly quotes. If it does, show the fix, and point out that the problem came from the copy, not the AI. See Smart Quotes From Copy and Paste.

Better prompt. Type the Prompt 2 block, which names the variables, the palette, the labels, the facets and the ggsave() size. Save the figure, and open it to check the labels and the legend.
Close. Ask learners to compare the ggsave() size with the value in the prompt.

title: Demo Script
text:
Episode 07: Statistics
Weak prompt. “Is there a relationship between bill length and bill depth in penguins? Give me R code.”. Type it, and show the answer.
What to point out.

The answer may give a confident yes or no, with no assumptions and no mention of grouping. See Wrong Statistical Interpretation.
Ask learners whether the answer mentions species. If it does not, note that the question is open-ended, and that is why the better prompt is needed.

Better prompt. Type the better prompt from episode 07, which asks for the pooled and the per-species fits, whether the two could disagree, and which variables could confound the relationship.
Simpson’s paradox. Show the pooled scatter plot first, then the per-species plot. Ask the AI what the pooled plot shows. A likely answer describes a negative relationship. Then show the coloured plot, and ask learners which answer they would put in the report. See Simpson’s Paradox.
Close. Ask learners to name one claim from the answer that they checked themselves.

title: Demo Script
text:
Episode 08: Assemble the Quarto Report
Weak prompt. “write a report about the penguins data”. Type it, and show the answer.
What to point out.

The answer may use a YAML header that does not match Quarto. Show the header and point to the format: key. See Outdated Quarto and R Markdown YAML.
The answer may stop before the end of the report. Use the truncation fallback if needed.

Better prompt. Type the Prompt 2 block, which asks for the section skeleton, the chunk options and the disclosure paragraph. Paste the skeleton into penguins_report.qmd, and render it with quarto render penguins_report.qmd.
Close. Open the rendered HTML and check that the AI-use statement matches the one learners drafted in episode 01.

title: Demo Script
section: Running Track B Alongside the Demo
text:
Running Track B Alongside the Demo
Track B learners work in Claude Code, in a terminal or the RStudio terminal, at the same time. Python learners on Track B start Claude Code with .venv active. The demo is for Track A, so keep it brief and return to the room.

Set a helper to circulate. The helper checks that each Track B learner has approved actions one at a time, and has not turned on auto-approval.

Check that no learner runs a loop, a background job or a polling command such as watch -n 1 squeue. These break the REANNZ agent rules in episode 02.
When a Track B learner finishes early, send them to the Check it step of the episode, then to extras/agent-track.md for the deeper material.
Show one Track B result on the screen at the close of episode 08, so Track A learners see what the agent extension produces.

title: Resources and References
text:
This page collects the books, guides, datasets, policies and documentation that the ML103 workshop draws on. Use it after the workshop to keep learning R or Python, to check a policy before you use an AI tool on NeSI systems, or to cite the workshop and its data.
Each entry gives the title, the authors or publisher and the year where known, and a line on why it helps with this workshop.

title: Resources and References
text:
Learning R and the tidyverse






Tip



Main next step after the workshop: R for Data Science (2e). Start here if you want to build on what you learned. It covers the same tidyverse tools you used in the workshop, with more depth and exercises.



R for Data Science (2e). Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Garrett Grolemund. O’Reilly, 2023. The free online book for the tidyverse workflow. These chapters match the workshop:

Data transformation: filtering, selecting, summarising and grouping, as in the dplyr steps of the analysis.
Data visualisation: the grammar of graphics behind the ggplot2 plots.
Quarto: writing reproducible reports, as in the penguins report.
Workflow: getting help: how to ask for help and write a good reprex when an AI answer does not run.

Introduction to R. Genomics Aotearoa. A free introductory course on base R, which the workshop assumes you already know.
tidyverse style guide. The naming, spacing and pipe conventions used in the workshop code.
ggplot2 documentation. Reference for every plotting function and argument, with examples you can run.
dplyr documentation. Reference for the data verbs such as filter(), mutate() and summarise().
Posit cheatsheets. One-page PDF references for the tidyverse and other Posit tools. Keep the dplyr and ggplot2 sheets next to your keyboard.

title: Resources and References
text:
Learning Python for data analysis
The Python version of the workshop uses pandas, seaborn and statsmodels. These resources cover the same ground.

Python for Data Analysis, 3rd edition. Wes McKinney. O’Reilly, 2022. The standard book on pandas, written by its creator. Read the chapters on data wrangling and plotting first.
pandas documentation. Reference for DataFrame methods, including the ones that replace dplyr verbs in the Python version.
seaborn tutorial. Introduces the statistical plots that the Python version uses for the penguins figures.
statsmodels documentation. Reference for linear models and their summary tables, as used for the body mass model.

title: Resources and References
text:
Reporting with Quarto
Quarto renders a single source file into HTML, PDF or Word documents, and runs R or Python code inside it. The workshop uses it for the penguins report.

Get started with Quarto. Installation and your first document. Follow it if Quarto is not already installed.
Quarto: R computations. How code cells, chunk options and figure sizes work for R.
Quarto: Python computations. The same options for Python code cells, including the Jupyter engine used in the Python version.
R Markdown. The earlier R reporting format that Quarto replaces. Use it only if you need to maintain an existing .Rmd file.

title: Resources and References
text:
The data
The workshop uses the Palmer Archipelago penguin data, collected by Kristen Gorman and colleagues at Palmer Station, Antarctica.

palmerpenguins package. Allison Horst, Alison Hill and Kristen Gorman. The R package that provides penguins. Use its documentation to check what each column means.
Horst AM, Hill AP, Gorman KB (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data. R package. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3960218. Cite this when you use the dataset.
Gorman KB, Williams TD, Fraser WR (2014). Ecological sexual dimorphism and environmental variability within a community of Antarctic penguins (genus Pygoscelis). PLoS ONE 9(3): e90081. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0090081. The original study that the data come from.







Note



R 4.5.0 and later include a smaller penguins dataset in the base datasets package, with different column names such as bill_len and body_mass. The workshop uses palmerpenguins::penguins. Check which one you have loaded with head(penguins).

Ethics, data sovereignty and research integrity

Guidelines for the best practice use of GenAI in research. Royal Society Te Apārangi, 2025. New Zealand guidance on the best practice use of generative AI in research. Read it before you put research data into any AI tool.
